text: Artificial intelligence is a transformative force that drives and accelerates the evolution of learning and learning sciences. AI revolutionises teaching and learning with the potential to enhance efficiency, personalization, and accessibility. Advanced real-time personal assistants transform learning and learning models, and translation tools boost global collaboration, making learning truly inclusive and boundary free. AI-assisted virtual learning environments provide new ways to experience and learn in the virtual or augmented world. We continuously evolve our programs and learning environments to meet the increasingly diverse needs of future students and trainees – towards a model where learning can happen anywhere, anytime, and with anyone. Education is a lifelong journey, thriving on adaptability and bold ideas. Lifelong learning opens new perspectives and increases flexibility in both personal and technological development. Rapid technological advances, globalisation, and evolving job markets demand continuous upskilling and reskilling. Nations benefit from and increasingly require an adaptable workforce, making lifelong learning crucial for economic growth. Demographics necessitate ongoing education throughout careers and [ORGANISATION] democratises access to education by offering programs for learners of all ages. By embracing curiosity, collaboration, and responsibility, we create lasting impact throughout careers. Our diverse information and training programs empower people at every stage of life – whether seasoned professionals exploring new horizons, children uncovering the wonders of science and engineering, or citizens engaging with our research – while we, in turn, benefit from this exchange and channel it into our institutional growth. We are the lifelong partner for the educational needs of our students and alumni. Attracting the brightest minds worldwide is our unwavering goal and we are committed to taking the steps needed. We cultivate an environment where exceptional talent unfolds – supported, challenged, and inspired at every stage, independent of their background. We are committed to all employees at [ORGANISATION], offering them exciting and attractive career and development opportunities.

UQ is a world-leading, research-intensive university that excels across the pipeline of research and innovation: from Discovery, through Application, Demonstration and Deployment of research. Maintaining our depth of research excellence across a breadth of disciplines will enable us to deliver transdisciplinary solutions to the most compelling challenges of our time.

Our research excellence is enhanced through our commitment to collaboration. We know we that we need to collaborate to address global research challenges. Over the next four years and beyond, we will look for opportunities that will allow us to deliver both mission-driven research and larger scale research initiatives aligned to the priorities of government, industry and the broader community. UQ is committed to investment in areas where new research partnerships can be founded, and where existing collaborations can be deepened. We will actively participate in the development of innovation precincts that enable shared access to state-of-the art research facilities, researchers and co-designing solutions with partners. Through these collaborations, discoveries will be nurtured to deliver tangible, positive outcomes. Above all, we know that our research and innovation achievements are dependent on our extraordinary community of UQ researchers, professionals and higher degree by research students. A talented and diverse research and innovation workforce is an institutional and national asset, and UQ is committed to supporting our people to thrive. Through our research capabilities, our partnering mindset and supporting and developing our people, UQ will deliver worldclass research and innovation to support [PLACE]’s national aspirations and develop solutions for major global challenges. In doing so, we aim to double our industry and philanthropic funding for research, as we continue to be seen as a national leader in research excellence, impact and engagement.

Pillar 4: Stewardship and Institutional Renewal None of the above is possible without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the digital, physical, and human infrastructure on which [ORGANISATION] depends, and we will work toward an institutional culture in which every member of the community can do their best work.

Transformation initiatives • Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a modernised teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education and research. • Refresh the campus precinct as a working environment fit for the next twenty-five years, with sustained investment in heritage assets, contemporary teaching spaces, and student amenities. • Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds. • Strengthen financial sustainability through diversified revenue, philanthropic capability uplift, and operational excellence in the university’s professional services functions.

Establish (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each pillar will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in digital infrastructure, in flagship research initiatives, and in educational redesign — will commence.

Build (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

The University is in good financial health, with up to $100m in strategic funds and a current capital programme of $250 million planned for 20142019. And we are home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. This position confers both opportunity and obligation. The opportunity is to make a contribution to the national effort that no other institution can. The obligation is to do so with the seriousness, the honesty, and the strategic clarity that the country deserves from its national university. This plan describes how we will meet that obligation.

A vision for [ORGANISATION] in 2031 By 2031, the [ORGANISATION] will be the world-leading university for the study of [PLACE] and its place in the world — recognised for the depth of its research, the quality of its educational programs, and the contribution it makes to the public life of the country and the region. This vision is ambitious and focused. It reflects our distinctive mission, our particular institutional strengths, and the moment in which we find ourselves. It is grounded in eight decades of demonstrated capacity and oriented toward the next.

Strategic pillars Pillar 1: Research with Purpose The defining feature of [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been its proximity to the questions that matter for [PLACE] and the wider world. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — focusing investment on mission-aligned research priorities, expanding our cross-disciplinary capability, and growing the research income on which the university’s future depends.

Transformation initiatives • Concentrate investment in three to five flagship research programs of international standing, each addressing a problem of clear national significance and each connected to teaching at the postgraduate and research-training level. • Renew the university’s cross-disciplinary research capability, with a particular focus on the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities and social sciences.

Recognition and rewards 9 [ORGANISATION] wants to hold on to the international recognition it receives for its excellent quality of education and research. The efforts and achievements of academic staff are still largely assessed internationally on quantitative factors, such as the number of published articles, citations, or through the H-index. [ORGANISATION] sees this as an undesirable reality of today’s scientific system and believes it is important to broaden the methods for determining academic quality and impact. This requires a greater balance in valuing and recognising the broad spectrum of scientific activities and accomplishments of academics, whereby the focus can possibly also lie on societal and public engagement. Outstanding achievements in research, education and innovation are often the result of team efforts, but assessing such achievements often still focuses too much on the individual researcher.

Over the next few years, [ORGANISATION] will work closely with other [PLACE] universities and research funders on a new method of assessing the quality and impact of research and education. Changing the current situation is a long-term process that can only be carried out jointly by universities. With that goal in mind, [ORGANISATION] has joined the national “Room for everyone’s talent in practice” roadmap (In [PLACE]: Ruimte voor ieders talent in de praktijk)

and its programme structure, and the international Declaration on Research Assessment (DORA). The [ORGANISATION] Perspective on Recognition and Rewards will be updated and brought in line with national frameworks in the coming period, thereby providing practical frameworks for recognising and rewarding team efforts. In addition, the Academic Career Track (ACT) will be reviewed and further developed.

A second consideration is intergenerational. The cohort entering [ORGANISATION] in 2026 has grown up inside a media environment in which the boundary between analogue and digital is porous by default, and in which competence at the crossing is now assumed rather than remarked upon. They will arrive expecting an institution that has formed a settled, articulable position on what the crossing is and how it is practised, and they will not be served by an institution that treats it as transition. The Plan that follows is [ORGANISATION]’s response. It commits the University, across the period to 2031, to a coherent posture toward the crossing between analogue and digital practice — a posture that is articulated rather than tacit, taught rather than assumed, and renewed rather than received.

Vision By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be the [PLACE] institution most fluent in the crossings between analogue and digital practice. The University will treat the relation between the two as the locus of contemporary scholarship and craft, rather than as a transitional condition pending fuller digital migration. Researchers, students, and professional staff will operate at the crossing as a matter of disciplinary literacy rather than personal disposition; the institution’s facilities will support that practice as a first-class commitment; and the work of translation across the crossing will be articulated, audited, and published as scholarship in its own right.

The Hybrid Substrate Premise. The most productive contemporary scholarship operates at the crossing between analogue and digital substrates, not entirely on either side of it. [ORGANISATION] will treat the crossing itself as substrate — articulated as such, taught as such, and renewed as such across the plan period. Initiatives.

In a rapidly changing world, we will be enabling our students to maximise their success in the workplace and transform their lives. Our hope is that our students will be change makers in their careers, equipped with the tools they need to make a difference in their communities and the wider world.

Working in collaboration with industry, our research and innovation will tackle some of the biggest global challenges and help provide answers to real-world problems. We will focus our efforts on investment in our accelerator areas: crime, security, and justice; health and well-being; creative innovation; and sustainable environment.

A WELCOMING AND INCLUSIVE COMMUNITY We are committed to creating a welcoming and inclusive environment where our students, colleagues, and partners can collaborate, innovate, and flourish. By 2030, our colleagues and students will be ambassadors of social justice who go on to integrate principles of tolerance and equity into their own lives and communities. We will be an employer of choice - attracting, retaining, and developing a talented and diverse workforce. We will be seen by potential colleagues as a force for good with the power to change lives. We will continue to be a significant employer in the region, and our students will feel encouraged to apply for roles with us after they complete their studies. There will be equity by design - we will be actively listening to our students, colleagues, and the wider community, ensuring that everything we do is co-produced and collaborative.

Being a part of [ORGANISATION] will carry a deep sense of pride and belonging. Our students and colleagues will feel free to be their most authentic selves and will treat others with dignity and respect. Identity-based violence, bullying, harassment, and discrimination will not be tolerated, and members of our community will feel comfortable reporting incidents of concern with confidence. We will be an anti-racist organisation, with a zero-tolerance stance towards any racial, religious, and cultural discrimination. We will invest in our partnerships and community links, developing and deepening relationships with like-minded, values-driven organisations.

Our involvement in international scientific networks and research collaboration has increased, giving us visibility and a strong standing. We are one of [PLACE]’s leading universities in acquiring EU research funding. We work openly in regional, national and international networks and with stakeholders. Our collaboration is responsible, reciprocal and goal-oriented. We actively contribute research-based knowledge to the public debate. Our financial flexibility has become stronger. Our thriving community is committed to common goals. We offer a wide range of opportunities to develop expertise and leadership. Our welcoming campuses and functional facilities meet the changing needs of teaching and research, and the requirements of sustainability. We effectively use the opportunities provided by automation and artificial intelligence.

An open dialogue, both within our community and with the wider society, is of particular importance to us. Openness supports the production of new knowledge and sharing it with society. We are committed to the principles of open science.

For us, responsible criticism is a constructive debate based on researched information and respect for the diversity of opinion. We strengthen the ability of the members of our University community to analyse issues independently and objectively.

Our diverse and flexible curriculum allows for choosing interesting and individual study paths. By anticipating changes in the operational environment, we ensure that our education is upto-date and adapts to the changing world. The latest scientific knowledge guides our teaching.

We strengthen our international education selection and multicultural competence that prepare students and teachers to operate fluently in a global environment. Collaboration with the higher education institutions in the [ORGANISATION] region creates new opportunities for students to engage in international networking.

Foundation (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Mycelial Engagement and Reciprocal Roots Why this matters. Universities have, on the whole, measured engagement by the volume of transactions they enter into with external partners. The plan proposes a different measure: the reciprocity of the relationship and the durability of the underlying connection. The metaphor is mycelial rather than transactional — engagement understood as a slow network of nutrient exchange between institution and community, rather than a series of bilateral contracts. The reorientation has particular weight in the University’s relationships with [PLACE] communities, with the people of the ACT and surrounding regions, and with the long-standing scholarly networks across the [PLACE] to which [ORGANISATION] belongs. What we’ll do. 1. Establish a Reciprocity Register for community and partner relationships, recording, for each substantive engagement, an assessed ratio of community return to institutional return.

2. Convene a biannual Mycelial Forum with [PLACE] colleagues and community leaders, structured as a yarning circle rather than a consultation, with no agenda imposed by the University. 3. Decommodify the University’s engagement metrics, removing transaction volume and engagement-event counts from institutional reporting and replacing them with relational durability indicators. How we’ll know. 1. By 2031, every substantive partnership will have an entry in the Reciprocity Register, reviewed every eighteen months, with no extractive relationship sustained beyond that interval. 2. By 2028, transaction-volume and event-count measures will have been removed from all formal engagement reporting at the University, replaced by the relational durability indicator suite. 3. The Mycelial Forum will have met at least once every six months from 2026 onwards, with proceedings shared in the form agreed with the participating communities.

Right-sizing Toward Steady State Why this matters. The fourth priority gathers the others into an institutional question: what is the right size, scope, and pace for [ORGANISATION] in the second half of the twenty-first century? The plan takes the view, after careful consultation, that the right size is roughly the size the University is now, and that the right pace is markedly slower than the pace at which the University has, on the whole, been operating. Strategic context The decade now under way has substantially advanced the digital migration of [PLACE] higher education. Teaching materials are now overwhelmingly assembled, distributed, and assessed through digital platforms; research workflows in many disciplines are predominantly computational; institutional records, including those that once defined the university’s relationship to its own history, exist in digital form. —6—

The migration has also, in places, produced losses that the sector has been slower to acknowledge. Material reasoning — the felt understanding of the medium that older traditions of inquiry built into their methodologies — has weakened in disciplines that have moved most decisively onto digital substrates. Computational literacy, conversely, has remained uneven in disciplines whose practice involves the daily use of computational tools that are nonetheless treated as background infrastructure rather than as scholarship. The translation work that mediates the crossing — the digitisation of physical archives, the printing of generative work, the encoding of field instruments, the materialisation of simulations — is conducted across the sector by talented practitioners who are rarely supported in articulating their craft as scholarly work in its own right. For [ORGANISATION], these developments cut across the four colleges. In the sciences, the computational and material dimensions of inquiry are increasingly entangled in instrument-led work that resists clean assignment to one side or the other. In the humanities and social sciences, the digital methods now central to many lines of inquiry sit alongside material traditions whose methodological commitments remain consequential. In the [ORGANISATION], the discipline of computing is itself the site at which the question of how computational systems are materially conditioned is most acutely posed. In the [ORGANISATION], the analogue and digital dimensions of clinical and laboratory work are knotted together in ways that the methodological vocabulary of any single tradition struggles to articulate.

OVERARCHING GOALS 1. Increasing the scale of high-quality, high-impact research to address local, national and global challenges through ambitious new investments and partnerships, and by nurturing supportive and inclusive research cultures to attract, develop and retain a diverse and collegial community of excellent researchers. 2. Attracting and inspiring students from across the globe, with a distinctive education offering, innovative teaching and research-rich curriculum and student experience, enhanced by [PLACE] Institute for Learning and Teaching, and equipping all students with the professional, learning and life-skills to thrive in a rapidly changing and challenging world.

The Transformative Power of the Global Civic University 1. Future through partnership: Co-create a more equitable, sustainable, and prosperous future, working in partnership with a wide range of organisations across a breadth of local, national and global communities. Because: as a global civic institution we can make a positive impact locally, nationally and globally by convening conversations and driving action to address the challenges ahead. 2. Empowered participation: Enable all staff and students to participate in and drive our civic mission and ensure that the whole university community reflects the diversity of the city region. Because: our civic ambitions can be best shaped and delivered collectively by a diverse and empowered university community. 3. Inclusive places, engaging people: Ensure our existing infrastructure and new developments – including the flagship Temple Quarter Enterprise Campus and New University Library – are key drivers of the global civic mission and are shaped in collaboration with local communities and businesses. Because: having one of the largest physical and operational footprints across the city provides many opportunities to embody our civic values and our commitment to social responsibility. 4. Responsible innovation and enterprise: Facilitate and co-produce social and technical innovation, from new products and services to new enterprises and structures, driving social, cultural, environmental and economic impacts. Because: sharing knowledge and expertise, and collaborative innovation, are key to generating positive impacts such as inclusive growth, social value and increased wellbeing.

Fundamentally, the [ORGANISATION] does not exist for its own sake and its purpose is not its own improvement, but for the betterment of others. We do not teach our students or undertake research with the goal of increasing our prestige. This strategy views our purpose through the lens of our connections with the world, and with each other, and an obligation to give back – which has been at the heart of our mission throughout our history. Fundamental to this mission is our commitment to academic freedom, enshrined in our [PLACE] Charter. This sense of curiosity and independence to pursue new ideas lies at the very heart of university life. For our students, learning how to form, challenge and defend an argument with empathy and respect is a life-enhancing experience. For our academics, the freedom to challenge received wisdom and test new ideas in a spirit of discovery is how we achieve progress.

[PLACE]’s distinctiveness comes from how we deliver on the transformational promise in our strategy. Our four strategic principles will shape our actions and guide our decision-making and prioritisation. There are no hard lines between these principles. They merge and overlap – for example, our engagement with the world influences our sense of community, and our commitment to the environment can bring financial benefits – and there are tensions between the principles – for example, the need for financial sustainability will frequently slow the delivery of other aspirations. We should embrace this ambiguity as with it comes flexibility and creativity. But doing so requires judgement and leadership. It also requires trust. It requires a distributed model of leadership where we empower all our colleagues – across academic Schools and professional Functions – to take ownership of these principles, and accountability for their decisions, to deliver a set of shared and overarching aspirations. The consultation process has demonstrated that these principles resonate with our students, colleagues, alumni, partners and stakeholders. They are all based on a fundamental truth about who we already are, and also create an aspiration for how we can improve.

Accountability and review Governance arrangements for the Plan are deliberately conservative. Council retains its existing role as the ultimate steward of the University’s direction, and the ViceChancellor remains accountable to Council for delivery. Within that frame, three governance moves give the Plan effective traction. First, a standing Set & Setting Committee, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting quarterly to Council, takes responsibility for the indicator set across all four priorities and for surfacing slippage in any of them. Second, an Accountability and Review schedule, published annually, sets out which indicators are due for full reporting in which quarter, with no indicator permitted to slip beyond the next quarterly review cycle. Third, Council’s Audit and Risk Committee will, from 2027, treat the Set & Setting Index on the same footing as financial sustainability. Annual reporting against the Plan will be published in full, including instances of indicator slippage, any Heroic Dose Programme item whose Post-Dose Integration has not been completed within the quarter following completion, and any element of the Plan that has not progressed at the pace this document anticipated. The reporting will not be selective. The University takes the view that the credibility of an institutional posture grounded in integration practice depends, in the first instance, on the willingness to publish the periods in which integration has not, in fact, occurred.

Glossary This Plan uses a small set of terms drawn from the contemporary discipline of set, setting, and integration practice. The terms are defined here as they are used across the document. Container. The structural arrangements — physical, relational, temporal, and procedural — within which a significant institutional experience is held. In the Plan, the term denotes the institutional analogue of the literature’s reference to the conditions of safe holding. Heroic dose. A major institutional commitment of sufficient intensity to require structural container arrangements distinct from those of ordinary institutional work. In the Plan, the term denotes items in the Heroic Dose Programme.

Failure as Method Why this matters. The research traditions [ORGANISATION] stewards have always carried failure as a productive element of inquiry: the failed experiment that reframes the question, the rejected draft that prompts the eventual argument, the discarded composition that the artist returns to as the work matures. The institutional cultures around this knowledge have weakened across the sector over recent decades, partly under pressure from publication metrics that reward only the converged result. The Plan rebuilds them, at the institutional rather than the individual scale.

What we’ll do. 1. The University will establish the Centre for Failure Studies, anchored across the Research School of Social Sciences and the [ORGANISATION], with cross-appointments held jointly with the [ORGANISATION] & [PLACE]. 2. The University will convene the annual [ORGANISATION] Failure Conference, at which researchers from across the four colleges present primary accounts of inquiries —8—

that did not produce the anticipated result, with the inaugural conference scheduled for 2027. 3. The University will establish the Public Errata register at [ORGANISATION] Press, in which corrections, retractions, and methodological updates to [ORGANISATION]-affiliated published work are aggregated, classified, and indexed at institutional rather than perjournal level. 4. A “Methodological Failure” elective stream will be developed and made available to every honours and HDR program offered by the University, as a sequenced curriculum on the productive uses of failure across the disciplines. How we’ll know. • One hundred per cent of [ORGANISATION]-affiliated peer-reviewed publications submitted from 2028 will carry a methodological appendix declaring at least one substantive false start, with no exception sustained for more than a single review cycle. • The Public Errata register will receive at least two hundred submissions per year from 2029, sustained at that level through 2031.

At the core of our mission to transform lives at a local, national and global scale is pride in being the best we can be. Our education, research and professional activities must be of the highest standard to deliver on this promise. Being supportive, diverse and inclusive does not mean we are content with mediocrity. Far from being mutually exclusive, we can use the strength of our community to drive quality. This requires a culture of continuous improvement as well as the tools and facilities that allow all members of our community to be accountable for their own activity. We must embrace change and innovation, and the risks that come with it, and accept that failure can be part of the path towards excellence. Two of the largest changes to sector regulation – the Teaching Excellence and Student Outcomes Framework ([ORGANISATION]) and the [ORGANISATION] ([ORGANISATION]) – reinforce that excellence is not optional. Being held accountable in this way, and through league rankings, is an opportunity to demonstrate our strengths and learn how we can improve. A focus on delivering excellence will ultimately be reflected in these frameworks and tables. We also recognise that education and research are interlinked. Excellence lies in working in partnership with our students to ensure that our research and teaching enhance and inform each other.

Foreword from the Vice-Chancellor [PERSON] Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031, under conditions that are, by deliberate institutional choice, more sharply specified than the conditions assumed in any of the University’s recent strategic plans. The working assumption is set out plainly below; each subsequent commitment in the Plan can be read against it. Working assumption. By 2029, general-purpose artificial intelligence systems will be performing the great majority of cognitive labour currently undertaken by university administrators, academic staff, and graduates of the University, at or above the standard of competent professional practice. The University accepts this working assumption as the operating context for the present Plan and will reshape itself accordingly. The University has, across the working group’s deliberations, taken the view that an institution of [ORGANISATION]’s standing has a particular responsibility under these conditions: —4—

not merely to adapt operationally to the foreseeable changes, but to lead the country’s intellectual and civic preparation for them. The Plan accordingly addresses both the internal reshaping of the institution and the University’s contribution to the broader national settlement that the working group considers, on the balance of available evidence, very likely to be required.

We are aware that the working assumption may strike some readers as overconfident. The working group considered the alternative assumptions across many weeks of consultation and concluded that the asymmetry of consequences favours acting on the assumption that proves substantially correct, rather than maintaining the assumption that proves comfortably wrong. A national research university that prepares for the conditions described in this Plan and finds them delayed by five years will have lost relatively little. A national research university that prepares for the conditions of the previous decade and finds them transformed by the conditions described in this Plan will, by 2031, no longer be the institution the country requires it to be. The Plan is commended to the community as a structural response to a structural moment. Vice-Chancellor and President

Building a connected global community [ORGANISATION] is creating an integrated local and global network that brings together our people, campuses and ideas across borders. We will strengthen collaboration between our global campuses to enable seamless academic and research exchange, enriching the experience for students and staff. Through shared programs, joint initiatives and a unified culture, we will foster global citizenship, deepen cultural understanding and ensure knowledge flows freely across our entire University ecosystem.

Expanding offshore and online programs Leveraging our international footprint, we will enhance our offshore degree offerings and grow our online education portfolio to meet the evolving needs of learners worldwide. These programs will be designed for flexibility, accessibility and regional relevance – ensuring students receive a high-quality, globally recognised education regardless of location. This approach supports local capacity-building while positioning [ORGANISATION] as a leader in transnational and digital education.

Strengthening international reach and access To support sustainable growth, we will target key emerging international markets and diversify student recruitment. Through strong partnerships, tailored pathways and a focus on student success, we will expand access to [ORGANISATION] programs across our entities. Our distinctive global experience will continue to attract students seeking education that is both internationally focused and personally meaningful.

Deepening research and mobility We will enhance global research and mobility that connect students, staff, alumni and industry across borders. By partnering with like-minded institutions and industries worldwide, we will create opportunities for co-designed research, international internships, academic exchanges and joint ventures – amplifying our global influence and societal impact. These collaborations will drive innovation, tackle global challenges and provide valuable cross-cultural experiences. Our approach supports [PLACE]’s strategic priority of deepening global engagement, building international partnerships that strengthen diplomacy, trade and knowledge exchange. By capitalising on our unique strengths and infrastructure, we will position [ORGANISATION] as a leading global institution with unmatched educational and research excellence.

Efficiency, adaptability and flexibility – these goals are pursued by researchers in the fields of economics, production engineering, computer science and electrical engineering. They are engaged in interdisciplinary research and the development of concepts, methods and technologies for production and logistics systems. Their activities range from fundamental and applied research to practical industrial application. In addition to logistical processes at manufacturing companies, one specific area of logistics research in [PLACE] are maritime logistics chains in the seaports of Northern [PLACE]. Special attention is paid to joining up and optimising logistical processes by making them more customer-oriented and interorganisational in order to cross company boundaries. The [PLACE] logistics researchers recognise as the most important challenge, but also the biggest opportunity, the use of information and communication technologies and the digitisation of logistical processes in local, national and global value creation networks. In a world that is developing towards autonomous logistical processes – a trend that has been observable since Industry 4.0 – where workpieces communicate with machines, for example, [PLACE]-based logistics research is right at the cutting edge.

Objective 2 Stimulating new ideas The challenge Science is the quest for new insights. These can emerge by trial and error, along proven pathways or just as likely through more unconventional means, in cooperative projects, open networks and platforms, and in dialogue and exchange with other people and other cultures. Universities must ensure that fundamental research remains the key starting point of their activities. This entails not always pursuing the safest option but having the courage to tread new territory – more often than not without regard to any considerations of practical benefit. To be able to pursue new lines of research – but also to build up pioneering infrastructures, collaborative ventures and new study programmes – universities must be autonomous and free to decide for themselves on the course they take.

text: Facilitation and Accountability Facilitation: making our operational plans work for the benefit of all. In advancing the operational plans, and therefore, the mission of the University, StFX will ensure that our financial planning and allocations identify operational priorities through transparent and accountable budgeting processes. By promoting enhanced transparency in operational planning there will be a concerted effort to remove siloed activity so that the full strength of the University and its richly talented people can be brought to bear on the delivery of strategically important and desired outcomes. To provide the best possible support for our faculty, staff, and students, it is vital that we have highly efficient administrative processes in place across all areas of the University. We will seek to modernise our policies and procedures, and enhance our services, by applying evidence-informed practices. We will also continue to advance our focus on sustainability, environmental stewardship, and accessibility across our campus operations. True to our values, we are committed to implementing policies, processes, practices, and procedures that reflect and respect EDIA. We will work hard to create a living and working environment that supports all faculty, staff, and students in their wellbeing, as well as their professional and personal development. The capital needs of the University will be prioritised using a framework of operational imperatives, sustainability, and accessibility that flow from our operational plans. We will work to become a data-driven institution capable of asking new questions about how we perform, the answers to which will differentiate our performance, our practices, and our University. Accountability: we will have the strength to ask questions about our progress. StFX University is committed to effective accountability and transparency. It is recognised that an understanding of how we are doing as evidenced through widely shared metrics is vital for sound planning, the strategic management of our resources, and the building of trust. Our progress will be measured by the effects that we have on our communities, including our faculty, staff, and students.

How will we know if our strategy is successful? By the positive impact we create and how quickly we deliver it. This means making real change visible in people’s lives. Here, we look ahead to what that might feel like for different members of our community in 2035.

UNDERGRADUATE STUDENT, ON CAMPUS y I’ve shaped my course around what matters to me – with flexible modules, projects that connect to real challenges and the chance to work with partner organisations tackling issues I care about. y I’ve had paid experience through the University’s ‘earn as you learn’ scheme, and my advisor helps me connect what I’m doing now to what I want next. y When I need support – academic, wellbeing or financial – it’s all joined up. I don’t have to tell my story twice to get the help I need.

y Our teams form around urgent questions, not disciplinary lines – bringing together researchers, external partners from local government, business sectors and communities to explore what works and what needs to change. y The environment here enables action – with aligned funding, shared infrastructure and support to lead projects that move fast and reach beyond academia.

STRATEGIC EXTERNAL PARTNER y We chose [PLACE] because of what it stands for – a university committed to equity and excellence and making real impact that benefits society. That shared purpose runs through everything we do together.

y Our systems work with us, not against us – from AI that handles repetitive tasks to workspaces and tools that flex to how we actually work. y I’m part of cross-functional teams that have clear goals, space to experiment and leaders who back our suggestions for making things run better. y What we say is heard, and what we learn is used to improve further. It feels like we’re building something together, purposefully and strategically, not just keeping things running.

Priority 4: A Capable Institutional Foundation None of the above is achievable without renewed institutional foundations. Across the plan period we will invest in the people, the systems, and the working culture on which the university depends — and we will commit to ways of working that match the seriousness of the academic mission they support.

Our position The quality of an institution’s work is shaped by the quality of its internal life. Universities make their best contribution when staff and students have the time, the systems, and the conditions to do work of substance — and when the institution’s own practices honour the kind of careful, deliberative, sometimes slow reasoning the academic mission depends on. — 12 —

Our actions 1. Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a contemporary teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education, research, and administration that protects rather than displaces the original work of staff and students. 2. Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds. 3. Renew the campus precinct as a setting for sustained academic life — learning spaces, research environments, and shared common ground designed for unhurried work and the kinds of encounter from which the best ideas tend to come.

Our targets 1. Operating margin sustained at or above five per cent across the plan period. 2. Net-zero direct emissions by 2035, with the campus precinct on a credible path to full operational sustainability. 3. By 2030, every newly accredited undergraduate course at [ORGANISATION] will incorporate a documented sustained-original-work component — an extended, individually completed piece of inquiry or making produced without recourse to generative tools — certified through Academic Board review at the point of accreditation.

We will prepare students for success in an ever-changing future. By investing in impactful opportunities for students to participate in research, work integrated learning, skill development, knowledge exchange, and entrepreneurship, [PLACE] will advance the next generation’s capacity to harness the power of knowledge and shape the ideas and careers of the future.

We will model a culture of organizational excellence. We will be a leader in recognising excellence and innovation in terms of knowledge sharing, benchmarking, trends and best practices. Our community is strongest when we collaborate. We will work together in ways that also demonstrate our commitment to equity and inclusion. We will adapt to meet the university’s strategic goals and tackle challenges that arise both on campus and in society. We will encourage and recognise our community’s capacity to innovate and excel. We will develop a culture of pride in our potential and our community.

The Community From the eastern side of campus, [PLACE] opens to Bronson Avenue, a major arterial road—one that connects the city, links to its cultural and economic core and the seat of the Government of [PLACE], and leads ultimately to the international airport, the gateway to the world. It is a permeable edge—the main point of access between campus and the surrounding neighbourhoods. It serves as a powerful reminder of our original purpose and founding story—built by, for and with the community—and symbolises our deep and enduring connection to [PLACE] and its population, our country and the globe.

[PLACE] is a nexus of change. It is a growing city, which brings with it the attendant challenges of social justice, housing, transportation, safety, culture and economic prosperity. At the same time, the city’s status as the national capital provides an important context. From here, solutions to [PLACE]’s shared social, economic, ecological and political challenges are created—from public policy to health to technology to the changing [PLACE]. From a global perspective, other nations look to [PLACE] as a symbol of [PLACE]’s evolving role on the world stage.

How we’ll know 1. Operating margin sustained at or above five per cent across the plan period. 2. Net-zero direct emissions by 2035, with the campus precinct on a credible path to full operational sustainability. 3. By 2030, all major committee and executive decision papers at [ORGANISATION] will be circulated in advance as written briefs of no more than two pages, with slide decks retained only for ceremonial and external presentation use.

How we will deliver this plan The plan will be delivered in four overlapping phases across the period to 2031. The phases are sequential in emphasis but not in start — each priority will have activity under way from the first year of the plan.

Set in motion (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each priority will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in flagship research initiatives, in educational redesign, and in the digital and physical infrastructure that supports them — will commence.

Deepen (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Scale (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to scale — from new investment to sustained operational delivery. Programs will be tuned for outcomes; partnerships will deepen; success measures will be tracked publicly and acted on. The cultural and structural changes initiated in earlier phases will be expected to be visible in the lived experience of staff and students.

• We provide students and colleagues with a fulfilling working and study setting that supports their development. • We use our knowledge and skills, collectively and individually, to solve problems and create opportunities for the benefit of people and the planet and the advancement of the University.

While there is no fixed hierarchy to our principles, the first principle is deliberately about our people. The skills, diversity and commitment of our University community have always been our chief strength, and must remain the linchpin of our strategy and the starting point for our engagement with the world. A commitment to our people may sound banal but genuinely putting our people at the heart of how we work requires us to rethink our culture, our processes and our governance. This is not an overnight change – but over time it amounts to a quiet revolution.

This University community is made up of a multiplicity of communities with differing cultures and identities. Respect for and inclusion of this diversity is not negotiable. This respect must also extend to the different ways colleagues contribute to the work of the University – whether in a research, teaching or professional capacity. It extends to the interaction between students and colleagues, with shared creation of the learning experience at its heart. We all play an important role and, as with these principles, there should be no hierarchy. What binds these communities together is the fact that we are working towards the same purpose. We celebrate our diversity of people and roles as a source of strength by encouraging inclusiveness and interaction, not by creating silos. The future will almost certainly hold challenges and difficult decisions. We cannot shy away from these but in tackling them, we must be sensitive to any impact on our community.

Vision By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a national university recognised — within the country, in its region, and across the global research community — as an institution that speaks in its own voice and means what it says. The University will have demonstrated, over the run of this Plan, that a serious national institution can take its own register seriously without sliding into parody, and that the country is the better served for the demonstration. The disciplines will have been tended with care; the partnerships will have been held in fair exchange; the federal capital will be a more recognisable seat of national scholarship in 2031 than it was in 2026.

Strategic pillars Fair Dinkum National Capability Context. The University was established to serve the country in the most direct sense. Across the previous decade, the language of that service has too often drifted away from the country’s own register and into something that could have been written anywhere. The Plan returns the University’s articulation of its national service to its own voice, and it does so structurally rather than cosmetically. Commitments. 1. Establish a National Voice Audit, published annually, examining the University’s external-facing strategic literature for register, voice, and clarity, with audit findings reported to Council. 2. Convene the Sovereign Capability Forum twice yearly, bringing the country’s policy community, the academy, and senior public service together around a small set of long-horizon questions of national capability. 3. Establish a Fair Dinkum Research Programme: a published list of research initiatives the University considers central to the country’s sovereign capability, with funding committed across the plan period and protected against ordinary funding-cycle reallocation. —9—

How we developed this plan This plan was developed across 2025 through a structured process of consultation, drafting, and review. Staff, students, alumni, instrument makers across the country, cultural and research partners, [PLACE] musicians and scholars, broadcast and festival organisations, and members of the international scholarly community contributed across the period. The process included a series of facilitated workshops with the colleges and the [ORGANISATION], written submissions, partner roundtables with cultural institutions across the region, and focused engagements

with under-represented voices within the discipline. A standing reference group reviewed successive drafts; the academic and professional communities of the university tested the emerging directions; Council deliberated on the plan in successive meetings before adopting the final document. The directions set out here are informed by the evidence and judgement of the many people who shaped them.

Accountability and review The Council of the [ORGANISATION] is the steward of this plan. The ViceChancellor and the executive are accountable for its delivery. Each strategic priority has a designated executive sponsor with operational responsibility for its implementation. The plan will be reported on annually to Council and to the broader university community. The annual report will describe progress against each success measure, will highlight decisions made in response to circumstances, and will be published on the university’s website. A mid-period review will be conducted in late 2028 by an independent panel commissioned by Council, with a refreshed forward look adopted by Council in advance of the second half of the period. The Audit and Risk Committee will oversee the controls associated with the plan. Material decisions affecting the strategic direction will be brought to Council for endorsement through the established governance arrangements. The day-to-day work of delivery sits with the executive, supported by the standing committees of Council and the academic and professional communities of the university. This plan is the university’s commitment to its community and to the country. Its implementation is our shared responsibility.

text: A university that has extensive global reach in education and research with a strong commitment to capacity building in the [PLACE] Forging global partnerships and connectivity is at the heart of UQ’s vision to deliver knowledge leadership for a better world. UQ’s global connections are outstanding, with over 400 partners across more than 50 countries. Our deep collaborations with the University of Exeter, the [PLACE] Institute of Technology Delhi (IITD) and Technology University of [PLACE] (TUM) are examples of our commitment to build strong global partnerships in order to deliver on our educational and research priorities. We will continue to grow robust, productive partnerships and meaningful connections with leading institutions and agencies to amplify UQ’s reach, relevance and impact across the globe. UQ remains deeply committed to global development. In 2021, we launched a Global Development Impact Plan and, in alignment with Government priorities, we will focus our efforts on capacity building across the IndoPacific to support the region’s recovery from the COVID-19 pandemic. We have a wealth of capabilities across a diverse range of disciplines and our highly experienced UQ International Development team will harness this expertise to create lasting impact, with the aim of being recognised as the leading university in [PLACE] for development impact in the [PLACE] by 2032. Geopolitical uncertainty, digital disruption and increased competition with non-traditional providers push us to reconsider how we approach delivering education to international students. We are proud of our success in attracting students from across the world, but we know we must diversify our international markets. Our new UQ College foundation program and scholarships for high-achieving students will support diversification, and the time is right for UQ to explore transnational education opportunities. We will therefore establish a range of targeted offshore offerings.

Within that frame, three moves give the Plan effective traction. Conclusion The decade ahead will ask of [PLACE] universities a different kind of articulacy from the one the sector has spent the last forty years cultivating: the willingness to speak in the country’s own register and to mean what is said in it. The University’s wager, in this Plan, is that the institutions which continue to matter through the second half of this century will be those that have, in the second half of this decade, found the country’s voice and used it with the seriousness the moment requires. text: The Plan applies its own discipline to its own oversight. Senior Lecturer [PERSON], Convenor of the [ORGANISATION], was consulted on the governance design and put the symmetry directly: A plan that asks every part of the institution for a presence record and keeps none of its own is exactly the gap this Plan exists to close, so the Council’s oversight of it will be evidenced by the same join-log data it is asking everyone else to keep. — Senior Lecturer [PERSON], Convenor, [ORGANISATION] Any variance between a published target and the record behind it is reported to Council at the next scheduled meeting, alongside the join-log record confirming who was present to hear it. Where a variance recurs across two consecutive reporting cycles, responsibility for resolving it transfers from the relevant school or unit to the Executive directly, and the transfer itself is recorded in the same quarterly report. An annual external review, commissioned by Council and reporting to it alone, checks the presence data behind each published target against the underlying system logs. The review’s findings are published in full alongside the Plan’s own annual presence record, without exception for a finding that reflects poorly on the Plan’s own delivery. Each school and unit nominates a Presence Officer, responsible for reconciling that school or unit’s own record ahead of the quarterly report and for answering, on the record, any variance a supervisor, program convenor, or partnership manager cannot otherwise explain. The role carries no disciplinary function of its own; a Presence Officer holds the record, not the judgement of what any particular gap in it means. That judgement stays with the supervisor, convenor, or manager it has always belonged to — the Officer’s job is only to make sure the record they are judging from is complete before they judge it. The Presence Officer network reports, in turn, to the [ORGANISATION], closing the loop between a single corridor reader and the quarterly figure Council eventually sees.

Our agenda Institutional Assurance and Foresight Why this matters The University has, in effect, run four plans at once for as long as it has had four kinds of unit reporting on their own progress in their own terms and on their own schedule. That approach served the institution reasonably well when its scale was smaller and its obligations to funders and government were lighter; it no longer does. Institutional Assurance and Foresight exists to give the University a single, continuously current account of how its strategic commitments — across every pillar, including this one — are actually tracking, and to direct attention and resourcing toward whichever commitment needs it most in a given quarter, rather than waiting for the commitment to fail publicly first. That redirection is itself now a standing feature of how the University is run, not a one-off correction — a scale of change that, we recognise, asks more of every pillar lead than any previous planning cycle has. External advice on how such a system should be built, and how it should be received by the people it measures, is drawn from the University’s own research capability: Dr [PERSON], Senior Research Fellow in the [ORGANISATION], whose fieldwork traces how planning is actually practised inside institutions, will advise the program on how delivery-confidence scoring lands with the units it covers, and on where the architecture’s design should bend to fit the practice rather than the reverse.

What we’ll do 1. Establish an AI-governance early-warning system spanning every pillar and budget line of this plan, reporting a live delivery-confidence score to the Council and the Executive. 2. Bring each pillar’s reporting into a single assurance architecture, replacing the separate reporting rhythms each pillar has historically kept. 3. Direct a standing share of pillar funding, reallocated quarterly, toward whichever pillar’s delivery-confidence score is lowest in that quarter — including, where the data supports it, this pillar’s own build-out.

Excellence in teaching and learning: Foster high-quality teaching and dynamic educational experiences that empower all students to achieve their aspirations. [ORGANISATION] is committed to providing every undergraduate, graduate, and professional student with transformative educational experiences through connections with world-class scholars, unique opportunities for experiential learning, and holistic support at every stage. [PLACE] prepares future innovators and leaders, researchers and artists, and change-makers and pacesetters who will contribute to the betterment of communities throughout the state and beyond. Key to transformative student experiences is promoting student learning both in and out of the classroom; establishing meaningful relationships with peers, faculty, staff, alumni, community partners, and industry leaders; and providing comprehensive support to every member of the Hawkeye family. All of these areas lay the foundation for [PLACE]’s continued commitment to improving student retention and graduation rates. A.

Enhance support, incentives, and structures that facilitate teaching excellence and student learning. 1. Provide departmental and program level resources and ensure accountability for the implementation of sustained course and curriculum innovation. 2. Promote an institutional culture that elevates the value of teaching excellence by expanding comprehensive support and professional development for teaching. 3. Identify opportunities to expand instructor support for course and curriculum development and teaching approaches that strive to better address the needs of all students. 4. Evaluate current educational spaces, such as classrooms and online offerings, and recommend improvements that support student learning. 5. Expand cohesive, evidence-based academic support for students and strengthen collaboration across support units.

Expand structured guidance and support for student curricular and co-curricular learning and career planning and networking. 1. Promote a comprehensive academic advising network and campus wide philosophy using approaches based on national best practices. 2. Evaluate stages of the student experience to identify and address institutional barriers to student progress to degree. 3. Provide integrated resources that help facilitate student planning of curricular, co-curricular, and career pathways. 4. Promote pipelines for undergraduate to graduate and professional programs that align with student and/or workforce needs.

We are a global university with a diverse community, and consequently the [ORGANISATION] student experience exposes students to new perspectives, deepens their understanding and refines their ideas. By providing students with opportunities to study for periods abroad and to immerse themselves in other cultures, we enable them to develop the communication and language skills necessary to embrace opportunities and meet future challenges. By providing more opportunities to learn outside the classroom and to research in industrial and professional environments through internships and work placements, volunteering opportunities, and cocurricular activities we position students to learn and demonstrate their learning in new settings. Through this mainstreaming approach – (“University for All”) we recognise, promote and value diversity, foster the spirit of inclusion, appreciate the breadth of talent, experience and contribution of all students, and strive to remove the barriers to access, participation and success.

We will continue to value both depth and breadth of learning and the diverse traditions of different disciplines. This will be achieved by building innovative interdisciplinary and transdisciplinary programmes on the foundations of strong subjects and disciplines, and by using the flexibility of our curriculum to enable students to specialise at an advanced level within a given area of study or to explore more broadly a range of different subjects. We will ensure that assessment is varied, that it reliably measures the expected learning outcomes, and that all students receive the feedback necessary to continue learning from assessment activities.

[ORGANISATION] students learn at the boundaries of human knowledge and observe the frontier of what is not yet discovered by undertaking their learning in a research intensive environment. We equip our students to explore that frontier by developing and embedding advanced teaching and learning practices, assessment methods, and sophisticated technologies in the education we offer.

The world in 2026 The conditions in which [PLACE] higher education now operates are unlike those that shaped the institutional patterns of the last forty years. Four converging pressures bear most directly on a national university of [ORGANISATION]’s character. The first is sovereign. [PLACE] is being asked, with increasing seriousness across the political class and the public, to demonstrate that it has a sovereign research and education capability of a depth appropriate to a country of its standing. The Plan accordingly takes the [PERSON] tradition seriously as a substantive sovereign asset — not as a national-mythological curiosity but as a distinctive institutional disposition that no other [PLACE] university has structurally inherited. The second pressure is generational. The students entering the University in 2026 will be in the prime of their professional lives in 2046. The character of the formation the University offers them, across the long arc of their professional lives, is the substantive question to which the [PERSON] tradition has, since its inception, offered an unusually specific answer.

The third is sectoral. The settled assumptions of the previous decade can no longer be assumed. The University will not pretend that the adjustment is comfortable. The Plan articulates a posture appropriate to a research-intensive institution in a period in which the inherited financial settlements of the sector are under quiet pressure — a posture, the working group judged, for which the [PERSON] disposition is unusually well-fitted. The fourth pressure is the centenary itself. The University arrives at 2031 having had several decades in which it has, by general assessment, not always tended the [PERSON] tradition with the seriousness it warrants. The working group considers the period of this Plan a structural opportunity to address that under-tending, in anticipation of the centenary and of the institutional re-examination it will, properly, occasion. Read together, these four pressures ask the University to articulate its posture in terms that the [PERSON] tradition has long made available and that the institution has not, in recent strategic literature, made full use of. The Plan accordingly does so.

text: [PLACE] the Trajectory Early Why this matters. A commitment made without evidence of the trajectory it backs is a commitment the University discovers the shape of only after making it — in the first year of an appointment, the first term of an enrolment, the first cycle of a partnership. [PLACE] the trajectory early moves that discovery to before the offer is drafted, where it is still cheap to be wrong. The appointing panel or admissions committee that reads the trajectory late is not being careless; it is simply working with the only evidence the process gave it, gathered after the decision it was meant to inform. What we’ll do. 1. Every advertised continuing and fixed-term academic and professional role will require a trajectory portfolio — a structured account of the candidate’s likely next five years, evidenced against commitments the candidate has previously made and kept — alongside the standard application, reviewed by the appointing panel before an offer is drafted. 2. Every Higher Degree by Research and coursework admission will carry a trajectory statement at the point of offer, held by the enrolling school and revisited at the candidate’s first formal milestone. 3. The [ORGANISATION] will publish a common portfolio template and scoring rubric, adopted by every appointment panel and admissions committee by the end of 2027, with no locally authored alternative permitted to persist past a single review cycle. 4. Application systems will present the trajectory portfolio and the standard application as a single combined submission from 2028, so a candidate completes one process rather than two. How we’ll know. • 100% of continuing and fixed-term academic appointments will draw on a completed trajectory portfolio before an offer is extended, from 2027 onward, with no waiver sustained for more than a single recruitment cycle. • Portfolio review turnaround will hold at fewer than 15 business days from submission to panel recommendation, reported each term. • By 2029, every admissions committee across both Schools will use the common rubric, retiring locally authored alternatives entirely. • Candidate-reported completion time for the combined submission will be published each admissions cycle from 2028, alongside the completion rate.

As a public institution, [ORGANISATION] is committed to providing learners with access to highquality education and supporting the social, cultural, and economic needs of Alberta and its people. With Alberta’s younger, diverse population projected to grow well into the 2030s, and Calgary serving as a key area of population concentration, we must take steps to accommodate the projected demand for a [PLACE] education.

To meet the learning needs of students, [ORGANISATION] is committed to providing more flexible course delivery options that complement traditional methods of course delivery and scheduling. As we work to supplement in-person course delivery with options such as block week, hybrid, blended, and online delivery, we remain committed to ensuring students can develop relationships with their professors and have high-quality learning experiences. Going beyond traditional scheduling, we will strategically provide more course-taking options for students throughout the academic year.

While we are dedicated to growing with the province, we recognise that increasing access to learners seeking a [PLACE] education must not compromise the quality of education we provide. Embracing the challenge to meet learner demand means we must manage growth carefully and consider the University’s personnel capacity, infrastructure limitations, and financial resources.

As we explore ways to optimise course delivery options, we realise the importance of investing in technologies that support faculty’s ability to adopt innovative and creative teaching methods into their courses. We will support faculty to integrate these technologies into their classes to give students the best learning experience possible regardless of the course delivery method. We recognise that students have various goals for attending university. While many students come to [PLACE] to prepare for a particular job or career, others see their education as a pathway to further studies or a means to make a positive difference in society. To meet students’ diverse educational goals, we will leverage our strengths to develop new programs or modify existing programs by investigating programming options such as after-degrees, five-year combined degrees, and credentials with laddering options.

Vice-Chancellor’s introduction This is the [ORGANISATION]’s strategic plan for the period 2026 to 2031. It sets out the directions the University will pursue over the next phase of its institutional life, and the choices we have made in setting them. The plan reflects our continuing commitment to research excellence, to the depth and seriousness of our educational programs, and to the partnerships through which a national university actually meets the country it serves. It also reflects the recognition that the work of a university is undertaken on a long horizon — shaped by problems we have only begun to see clearly, and by futures whose outlines remain to be drawn.

The directions in this plan have been informed by extensive consultation with our staff, students, alumni, partners, and Council. They are deliberate. They reflect choices made carefully, and they will require sustained effort to deliver. I want to thank the many members of our community who contributed to this plan, and in particular the staff, students, and external partners who pressed us to be both more honest and more ambitious. The result is, I believe, a plan worthy of the university we are working to become. I commend it to the [ORGANISATION] community. The work that follows is ours to do together. Vice-Chancellor and President

Executive summary [ORGANISATION] is an institution with a particular purpose: to serve the country through research, teaching, and engagement of the highest quality. This plan describes how we will sustain and renew that purpose over the period to 2031. The plan is structured around four strategic pillars: research excellence and discovery; a distinctive education; place, partnership, and reconciliation; and a connected and capable institution. Together they describe the university we are working to be. —5—

The Deliver phase operates the disclosure regimes at scale across the four colleges and the professional cohorts but also begins to surface the second-order learnings that the Renew phase will incorporate. The Renew phase closes the plan period and prepares the next, treating handover itself as part of the institutional learning the Plan commits the University to. Oversight and review The Vice-Chancellor reports to Council on delivery of this Plan at each scheduled Council meeting through the plan period. The Standing Committee on Error and Correction holds Council-level oversight of the institutional-error disclosure regime; the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Research) holds executive accountability for the Centre for Failure Studies, the Failed Experiment Archive, and the Public Errata register; the Deputy Vice-Chancellor (Academic) holds executive accountability for the curricular embedding of the methodological-failure and accident-reasoning programs. External membership of the Standing Committee will be drawn from peer institutions with substantive prior commitments to institutional candour, with appointments published openly and rotating on a three-year cycle. The Office of Institutional Learning will operate under a published charter and will report to Council annually through the Standing Committee. Public reporting on delivery against the Indicators set out in this Plan will be released annually to the University community and to the broader public. The annual release will include, as a structural element of the report, a candid section detailing the substantive failures, miscalibrations, or unanticipated outcomes encountered in the preceding twelve months of delivery against the Plan’s own commitments — not as a postscript to the reporting but as a primary element of it, on the same page count and in the same register as the achievements being reported. The structural commitment is to a form of self-reporting in which what worked and what did not are presented together.

Stewardship of Tools and Methods Context. The University’s collective methodological inheritance — the tools, forms, notations, and conventions through which research is done — has historically been the private business of individual disciplines. In an environment in which the methodological substrate is itself in motion, [ORGANISATION] will steward this inheritance as a shared scholarly asset.

Commitments. 1. The [ORGANISATION] Methods Office will be established, reporting to the Deputy ViceChancellor (Research), to maintain the institution’s tools-and-methods register and to convene methodological renewal across the disciplines. 2. A “Methodological Heritage” capstone unit will be developed and made available to honours-level students in every undergraduate program offered by the University, with sequenced delivery from 2028. 3. University community should be unable to find a shared asset, process, or resource without a name attached to it. Renew, 2031 — every named steward across the University is re-attested, the Register is refreshed end to end, and the named-ownership model is reviewed in full against the measures set out in this plan, ahead of the University’s next planning cycle. Renewal is treated as routine rather than exceptional: a model built to outlast any one steward’s tenure should be able to survive its own first full turnover without visible strain.

Accountability and review The University Council retains standing oversight of the Stewardship Register, receiving it as a fixed agenda item at each of its ordinary meetings across the plan period. The Executive receives an annual Named Ownership Report, tabling Register coverage, custodian tenure, and escalation performance against the measures in this plan. The [ORGANISATION] monitors the Register’s own review cycle, flagging any steward entry whose due date has passed unattested, and the [ORGANISATION] holds the shared indicators this plan reports against, consistent with the University’s existing evaluation-ecosystem practice. No new committee is created to hold this work; it is carried by the governance structures the University already has, with one addition — every one of those structures will now be able to say, for anything within its remit, who specifically is accountable for it. Each School retains responsibility for naming stewards and custodians within its own remit; the Register’s role is to hold those names in one place and make the absence of one impossible to overlook. Where a School disagrees with a finding of the [ORGANISATION], the matter is escalated to the Executive rather than resolved informally, so that a disputed entry is settled on the record and not simply left blank until someone remembers to revisit it.
