Building for the Future In a landmark development for our university and city, we are building a new Library and Learning Commons at the heart of our campus. This purpose-built facility will transform student, staff and public engagement in our learning resources, technologies and academic skills. After 175 years of university education in [ORGANISATION], it marks an exciting new chapter in how we engage with knowledge and discovery. This flagship building will be located beside the city’s Quincentennial Bridge and it will act as a beacon of learning for our university city. It is designed to be an inspirational, welcoming, high-tech space of learning and creativity that brings diverse people and disciplines together. We look forward to it becoming a vibrant scholarly and social space for [ORGANISATION].

By 2035, we will be counted among the Top 200 universities globally in at least one established World University Ranking. This target demonstrates our ambition to be a highly effective organisation, recognised for our high standards of research excellence and global impact.

We will be a university of choice that inspires and supports its students across their learning journey to become outstanding graduates. This target demonstrates our ambition to focus collective effort to improve student progression, academic engagement, teaching excellence, wellbeing and belonging.

Strategy Implementation Together, we have set out an ambitious shared vision for our university in the coming years. Realising this ambition will require institutional focus to ensure that decision-making at all levels supports delivery and that strategic financial planning and revenue growth align with our priorities.

Our Colleges are at the heart of our vision and they are the key drivers of research and teaching excellence. Each of our four Colleges will publish their own College level strategies identifying where and how they will contribute to us achieving our collective vision for the University. Implementation of these actions will be monitored over time through our Colleges’ rolling five-year business plans, and School and Research Institute annual operational plans.

Third, judgement-based assurance is already the sector’s quiet practice. Peer review, examiners’ reports, promotion committees, and accreditation panels all rest, in the final instance, on the trained sense of the people in the room; the surrounding documentation records the judgement rather than producing it. This Plan does not introduce felt sense into the University’s assurance arrangements. It acknowledges the position felt sense already occupies, and resources it accordingly. Fourth, the University holds a distinctive institutional capability in this domain. The [ORGANISATION] brings two decades of scholarship on evaluation ecosystems and metric stewardship; the [ORGANISATION] brings the anticipatory and foresight practices through which an institution senses conditions before they are recorded. Few institutions are better placed to make attunement rigorous, and the University regards the opportunity as strategic rather than incidental. Read together, these features ask the University for a deliberate posture rather than an incremental one. The posture this Plan adopts is set out in the ambition that follows. —6—

Our ambition By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be the institution whose quality is assured by the calibrated, collective, and accountable felt sense of its own community. Quality at the University will be something its practitioners recognise together, in structured settings, on the record, and at the point where quality is made rather than where it is later documented. The instruments that once stood in for that recognition will have been honourably retired; the community that replaces them will be accredited, renewed, and trusted — inside the institution and beyond it — to know good work when it feels it.

Integration. The slow embedding of an experience or finding into the working understanding of the institution, distinguished from the experience itself. The Plan treats integration as a substantive institutional discipline. Microdose. A sub-perceptual dose; in the Plan, a low-intensity, regularly administered formation-oriented seminar distributed across the long arc of a degree. Set. The mindset, intention, and preparation with which the University approaches a given inquiry. The first of the two classical terms the Plan invokes. Setting. The physical, relational, and temporal conditions in which inquiry is conducted. The second of the two classical terms the Plan invokes. Sub-perceptual dose. A dose at a level below the threshold of immediate perception but sufficient, when regularly administered, to produce durable formation. In the Plan, the term denotes the principle underlying the Microdose Curriculum.

Looking ahead The decade ahead will ask of universities a different kind of attention from the one the sector has spent the previous forty years cultivating: the willingness to take seriously the conditions under which inquiry produces durable understanding, rather than the willingness to multiply the inquiries themselves. The University’s wager, in this Plan, is that the institutions which continue to matter through the second half of this century will be those that have, in the second half of this decade, attended to set, setting, container, and integration with the seriousness the contemporary literature recommends. The work is patient and largely invisible from outside. Much of it is the slow work of preparation, of holding, and of integration that no audience ever sees directly. But the conditions on which a national research university’s contribution to the country depends are not built in any other way. The medicine, properly held, integrates. [ORGANISATION] will continue the work of holding it.

text: Roadmap The plan will be delivered in four overlapping phases across the period 2026 to 2031. The phasing reflects the realistic pace at which a research-intensive national university can stand up a capability of this scale, and the differing time horizons over which the priorities will mature. Each phase has its own emphasis; none stand alone. Set in motion (2026). The first year is a year of groundwork. Implementation arrangements are stood up, baseline measures are confirmed, the consultation and partnership settings on which the plan depends are renewed, and the early actions in each priority are set in motion. The end-of-year review establishes the conditions for a stronger build phase. Deepen (2027–2028). The middle years of the early period are the years of substantive build. Initiatives in each priority move from establishment into delivery; the cross-disciplinary research programme reaches operating maturity; the public performance programme begins to take its sustained shape; the precinct consolidation reaches its first major milestones. The mid-period review is undertaken in late 2028. Scale (2029–2030). The later years of the plan period are the years in which the directions set out here are scaled into the institutional fabric. The Archive opens and accepts its first acquisitions; the fabrication and acoustic capability reaches sustained operating scale; the undergraduate studio cycle is integrated across the colleges; the partnership programme reaches its planned breadth. Sustain (2031). The final year is a year of consolidation and forward look. The plan and its initiatives are reviewed against the evidence of the preceding years; the directions for the period beyond 2031 are settled in the light of what has been learned; the foundations for the next strategic cycle are laid.

Each phase has its own emphasis; none stand alone. Set in motion (2026). The first year is a year of groundwork. Implementation arrangements are stood up, baseline measures are confirmed, the consultation and partnership settings on which the plan depends are renewed, and the early actions in each priority are set in motion. The end-of-year review establishes the conditions for a stronger build phase. Deepen (2027–2028). The middle years of the early period are the years of substantive build. Initiatives in each priority move from establishment into delivery; the cross-disciplinary research programme reaches operating maturity; the public performance programme begins to take its sustained shape; the precinct consolidation reaches its first major milestones. The mid-period review is undertaken in late 2028. Scale (2029–2030). The later years of the plan period are the years in which the directions set out here are scaled into the institutional fabric. The Archive opens and accepts its first acquisitions; the fabrication and acoustic capability reaches sustained operating scale; the undergraduate studio cycle is integrated across the colleges; the partnership programme reaches its planned breadth. Sustain (2031). The final year is a year of consolidation and forward look. The plan and its initiatives are reviewed against the evidence of the preceding years; the directions for the period beyond 2031 are settled in the light of what has been learned; the foundations for the next strategic cycle are laid.

Objective 6 Developing staff potential The challenge Motivated and competent staff are the prerequisite for ensuring that an organisation can realise its ambitions. Universities seeking to attract and retain highly qualified and committed people in research, teaching, innovation and public engagement, continuing education, technical services, administration and management need to enable participation and equal opportunity, ensure information and involvement, and provide good working conditions and reliable career prospects. This calls for a holistic approach to diversity, leadership and organisation. In order to be successful, universities must ensure that all members of the institution are able to develop their potential to the full.

Objective 7 Building bridges to the world The challenge Global networking as a result of digitalisation, [PLACE] programmes, international partnerships and alliances as well as international rankings are just a few of the highly diverse aspects that characterise the worldwide scientific community today. Over the past few decades, science and academic education, especially in the [PLACE] Union, have benefitted to an unprecedented extent from increasing cross-border cooperation and easier international access. Nevertheless, open international exchange among academics and academic freedom are at risk wherever democratic values are flouted. Universities consistently build bridges by cultivating personal contact and establishing joint programmes based on clear standards in the areas of research, the promotion of early-career researchers, and study programmes.

Cooperation is integral to science – internationally, regionally, with colleagues from other academic institutions and with private enterprises as well as societal actors. Especially within the local region, manifold opportunities exist to complement competences and develop synergies in close cooperation based on mutual trust. In the face of today’s growing demands on research and education, it is possible to benefit mutually from cooperation in the areas of teaching and learning, research and development, innovation and public engagement. Moreover, changes in the law and in funding policies within the [PLACE] science system will impact on the collaboration between universities and non-university research institutions in future years. The universities are in a position to help shape this process.

Research with Impact The bedrock of [ORGANISATION]’s global reputation for impact is the extraordinary strength of our research. We will be recognised as a world-leading university, and collaborative partner of choice, founded on the excellence and transformative impact of our research. Our global reach will be recognised, and our social purpose will also champion the delivery of prosperity, jobs and well-being to our local and regional communities. We value basic, curiosity-driven research as a driver of discovery. We will build on these knowledge foundations to develop new ideas and theories, continuing to develop design-led innovations addressing global challenges in the fields of health, education, sustainability, and social justice.

Education and Student Experience We will offer a world-leading education and student experience through a blend of traditional programmes, stackable qualifications, and micro-credentials, with flexibility and support to learn on campus, through blended learning or online. Our programmes will develop skills and will support work-based learning to maximise the opportunity for students to move into the world of work. Our learning and teaching will be student-focused, delivering the best possible student experience and work-ready students equipped for the world that they are destined to shape. To support their development as change-makers, our students will be encouraged to help develop and define the values of the university. Through this ongoing endeavour students will be empowered to help us create and deliver a smooth and seamless student experience from the point of initial enquiry to graduation and beyond, as alumni and continuing members of our community. Our approach throughout development and delivery of learning and teaching in [ORGANISATION], Kirkcaldy, and internationally will be through meaningful and sustained partnerships. This is the commitment that underpins our enabling strategy on Education and Student Experience.

text: At UQ, our success depends on the talent, creativity and dedication of our people. We support staff by developing their skills and talents, encouraging personal and professional growth and creating opportunities for leadership and impact within and beyond the University. We aim to cultivate an environment that promotes equity, diversity and inclusion, where everyone is valued, respected and able to thrive. As digital and technological change becomes more central to our work, we will equip staff with the skills, confidence and ethical frameworks needed to navigate both opportunities and risks. By strengthening capabilities such as critical thinking, creativity, empathy, intuition and ethical judgment, we will support staff to use AI strategically. This approach will be guided by responsible-use frameworks, strong governance and equitable access to tools and resources. We are committed to developing career pathways and strengthening leadership skills for both academic and professional staff. Building on the initiatives such as our Leadership Framework, the Study for Staff program and the creation of Teaching Associate roles, we aim to build the capabilities required for UQ’s future workforce. We are also committed to ensuring that UQ reflects societal diversity and values the varied experiences, perspectives and knowledge of our people. We will apply an intersectional perspective to our equity, diversity and inclusion efforts to ensure no one is left behind, while fostering safe and supportive environments for all staff. Our priorities include increasing the representation of women and [PLACE] and [PLACE] peoples – particularly in senior leadership roles, implementing anti-racism initiatives, eliminating UQ’s gender pay gap, addressing psychological safety and removing barriers for people with disability and the neurodivergent community.

text:
Executive summary This Strategic Plan commits [ORGANISATION], across the period 2026-2031, to a single organising idea: that no AI-assisted recommendation affecting a student, staff member, or applicant should take effect without a named person attesting that they have read it and stand behind it. Four strategic priorities carry that commitment from the decision itself through to the capacity to review it, the public’s standing to ask about it, and its survival as the number of such decisions keeps rising.

Together these priorities move the University from a default in which an AI-assisted recommendation is actioned unless someone happens to object, to a default in which it is actioned only once someone specific has attested to it. The initiatives that follow are specific by design: each carries a target, a date, and a mechanism for knowing whether it has been met. Where earlier plans have asked the University to “govern AI responsibly” in the abstract, this plan asks something narrower and considerably harder to fake: that every such decision have exactly one name against it, and that the name mean something. None of the four priorities invents a discipline the University does not already practise somewhere. Each extends a habit already at work in one part of the institution — a named convenor, an attested custodian, a published register — to the specific and fast-growing case of decisions an AI-assisted tool has helped make. That is a deliberate choice: an institution that already knows how to name someone accountable for a research instrument does not need a new capability to do the same for a rostering flag, only the will to apply the existing one without exception, at a volume the existing one was not originally built for. The remainder of this document sets out the operating environment that makes this commitment necessary, the ambition that follows from it, and the four strategic priorities, their initiatives, and their measures in detail, before closing with the phasing, governance, and review arrangements that will carry the plan through to 2031.

Promote institutional excellence and success by attracting and recruiting a talented body of students, faculty, and staff to create a welcoming and engaged community that is rich in diversity of backgrounds, perspectives, viewpoints, and experiences. 1. Recruit talented undergraduate, graduate, and professional students. 2. Recruit exceptional faculty, with a focus on areas of strategic importance. 3. Recruit talented staff, with attention to areas of critical need to the institution.

Retain talented faculty and staff through professional development, recognition, and a culture of connection and employee value. 1. Identify and address gaps in faculty and staff satisfaction within the career lifecycle. 2. Ensure access to training and professional development and clarify pathways to career advancement. 3. Identify internal and external opportunities for cultivating emerging leaders and provide training and mentoring to expand leadership skills. 4. Identify opportunities to enhance supervisor development. 5. Review reward and incentive structures and make recommendations to increase recognition of excellence in key areas that support strategic priorities. 6. Assess the potential impact of innovative workplace strategies, such as flexible work practices on staff recruitment and retention.

Explore improvements in infrastructure—including people, processes, policies, and technology—to support faculty, staff, and campus leadership in using institutional data to plan, implement, and assess efforts to advance individual and institutional success. 1. Cultivate a campus culture of data-informed assessment and continuous improvement. 2. Identify the needs of information users that are not being addressed by existing information resources and infrastructure, including potential enhancements to data collection and reporting tools. 3. Examine the feasibility of creating a central hub for institutional data and assessment coordination to support data literacy and data-driven decision making.

Our targets 1. [PLACE] student enrolments to double by 2031. 2. [PLACE] staff representation to double across academic and professional roles by 2031. 3. By 2030, every flagship [ORGANISATION] research initiative addressing a question of national significance will run at least one structured decision-rehearsal exercise per year, jointly designed with [PLACE] or partner agency it serves, with the methodology and participant cohort published openly.

Priority 4: A Connected and Capable Institution None of the above is achievable without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the people, the systems, and the working culture on which the university depends — and we will commit to ways of working that match the seriousness of the academic mission they support.

Our position The quality of an institution’s work is shaped by the quality of its internal life. Universities make their best contribution when staff have the time, the systems, and the conditions to do work of substance — and when the institution’s own practices honour the kind of careful, deliberative reasoning the academic mission depends on.

Our actions 1. Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a contemporary teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education, research, and administration. 2. Build a standing institutional capacity for scenario-based planning and structured exercises, drawing on the university’s strengths in policy, security studies, and complex-systems research, and shared with partner agencies through the National Security College and related platforms. 3. Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds.

A Community of Calibrated Feel Why this matters. Attunement is a capability of people, and it is only an institutional capability when the people who hold it are many, aligned, and renewed. A felt sense that lives in a handful of senior practitioners is a dependency, not an assurance arrangement. The third priority therefore builds the community: accredited practitioners across every school and portfolio, a shared sensibility maintained through deliberate calibration, and a pipeline through which the feel is passed on faster than it retires. What we’ll do. 1. Develop and deliver Foundations of Vibe Literacy, an accredited program through which every continuing staff member acquires the shared vocabulary, calibration practices, and recording conventions of structured attunement. 2. Establish a practitioner accreditation pathway, from foundation through panel ready to senior practitioner, with progression assessed — appropriately — by attunement, and with senior accreditation renewed through participation in calibration convenings. 3. Build calibration into the institutional rhythm, through regular cross-school convenings in which practitioners re-align their reads against shared cases, drawing on the [ORGANISATION] line where an intensive format serves the cohort. 4. Recruit and promote for feel, incorporating demonstrated attunement capability into academic and professional promotion criteria and into selection for institutional leadership roles. How we’ll know. — 10 —

• All continuing academic and professional staff will hold Foundations of Vibe Literacy accreditation by the end of 2029, sustained at 100% of the continuing cohort thereafter. • The community of panel-ready practitioners will at least double over the plan period, with completions across the accreditation pathway in the low thousands. • By 2031, the University will maintain at least 80 strategic partnerships with organisations whose quality cultures it judges, on attunement, to be compatible with its own.

text:
We live in an era of disruptive change in which the pace of technological innovation is remarkable. Unprecedented access to information is redefining the ways we live, learn and work. As a university, we must rise to the challenge of preparing our graduates for success in a future that will be every bit as dynamic and unpredictable as it is exciting.

This means challenging traditional paradigms and embracing the emerging opportunities. Challenging times require courage, vision and purpose, all of which have been hallmarks of [PLACE] since its inception 50 years ago. Our namesake, Matthew [PLACE], was a man of purpose. When asked why he chose to embark on his incredible voyage of discovery he responded, “I have too much ambition to rest in the unnoticed middle order of mankind”. He was also a man who believed in the importance of actions that “speak to the world” and this commitment is reflected in our new Strategic Plan Making a Difference – the 2025 Agenda. It sets out an ambitious vision for [ORGANISATION]. One that will harness disruptive technologies and chart a course that takes us to the top 10 of [PLACE] universities and the top one percent in the world.

Implementing our vision requires a set of specific metrics against which to monitor progress. These will be applied throughout our organisational structures so that all staff can see how their own efforts contribute towards our vision. These metrics will be complemented by a Planning and Accountability cycle that will enable us to recognise achievement and modulate plans to promote continuous improvement. A shared sense of purpose, together with a common set of values, is fundamental to a successful culture. Following university wide consultation with staff and students, four core values have emerged – Integrity, Courage, Innovation and Excellence, and above all an ethos that is Student Centred. We will continue to consult with staff and students as we articulate how these values will manifest in our day-to-day experiences at [PLACE].

The third is geopolitical. The strategic environment in which [PLACE] operates has become more contested, more uncertain, and more consequential for the country’s future. [PLACE] universities are increasingly being asked to support a broader, more deliberately diversified set of international partnerships — particularly across the [PLACE], and with [PLACE] partners with whom [PLACE] shares both research traditions and strategic interests. [ORGANISATION] is well placed to lead in this work, but doing so well will require sustained and intentional effort across the plan period.

Within this environment, [ORGANISATION] sits in a particular position. We are the country’s national university, research-intensive at a scale and depth unmatched in [PLACE], and home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. We are anchored in [PLACE], a city whose institutional fabric is closely entwined with our own, and connected through long-standing relationships with peer institutions across the world. This position confers both opportunity and obligation. The opportunity is to make a contribution to the national effort that no other institution can. The obligation is to do so with the seriousness, the focus, and the strategic clarity that the country deserves from its national university. This plan is our response.

Our ambition By 2031, the [ORGANISATION] will be the world’s leading university for the study of [PLACE] and its place in the world — recognised for the depth and quality of its research, the formation of its graduates, and the contribution it makes to the public life of the country and the region. This ambition is deliberate. It draws on the particular history and mission of [ORGANISATION], on the strengths we have accumulated across eight decades, and on a clear-eyed read of the contributions [PLACE] and the world will need from a national university over the decade to come. It is grounded in what we already do well, and oriented toward what we are working to become.

equivalent maturation is more recent and more fragmentary: the institutions have not yet collectively decided what an articulated practice of error and accident looks like for an interpretive or compositional tradition. In the [ORGANISATION], the question becomes acute: the disciplines housed there both produce the generative systems whose failures preoccupy the public and develop the methodological tools through which those failures are studied. And across the University’s professional cohorts, the wider conversation about institutional candour places new demands on the disclosure and learning practices through which the institution governs itself. The University is well placed to lead, but only on the condition that it is willing to organise itself around the proposition that being a research university involves being wrong, often, in particular and disciplined ways. The Plan that follows is the University’s commitment to do so.

What we will become By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be the [PLACE] university most attentive to its own errors, glitches, and accidents, across teaching, research, and operations. The University will treat these as primary sources of institutional learning rather than departures from a smoother norm. Researchers will publish into a methodological environment in which a substantive false start is a declared element of the work rather than an item edited out before submission; students will graduate from coursework in which the productive uses of failure are part of the explicit curriculum rather than picked up tacitly from a supervisor; and the institution will report annually on its own significant mistakes, near-misses, and corrections at the same cadence and with the same seriousness as it reports on its financial position.

A distinctive position [ORGANISATION] sits in a particular position. We are [PLACE]’s national university, established by an Act of [PLACE] [ORGANISATION] with a charter to serve the nation. We are research-intensive at a scale and depth unmatched in the country. And we are home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. This position confers both opportunity and obligation. The opportunity is to make a contribution to the national effort that no other institution can. The obligation is to do so with the seriousness, the honesty, and the strategic clarity that the country deserves from its national university.

This vision is ambitious and focused. It reflects our distinctive mission, our particular institutional strengths, and the moment in which we find ourselves. It is grounded in eight decades of demonstrated capacity, and oriented toward the next.

Strategic pillars Pillar 1: Research Excellence and National Impact The defining feature of [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been its proximity to the questions that matter for [PLACE] and the wider world. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — focusing investment on mission-aligned research priorities, expanding our cross-disciplinary capability, and growing the research income on which the university’s future depends.

• Renew the university’s cross-disciplinary research capability, with a particular focus on the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities and social sciences. • Establish a national institute drawing together [ORGANISATION]’s distinctive strengths in equine genomics, livestock-systems modelling, and the environmental history of the [PLACE] pastoral economy — a vehicle through which the university’s research effort can be aligned with one of the country’s most enduring industrial and cultural traditions. • Strengthen the institutional supports for research integrity, research data, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence in research, ensuring that [ORGANISATION]’s research practice continues to set the standard for the sector.

How we’ll know • By 2028, 100% of pillar-level budget lines across the plan will be visible to the early-warning system in real time, with no exception sustained for more than a single reporting cycle. • By 2029, the median time between a delivery risk emerging and its appearing on the Council’s assurance dashboard will fall under one reporting cycle. • By 2031, at least one full cycle of quarterly reallocation will have been completed without a pillar’s delivery-confidence score requiring escalation to external review.

Research Excellence and Discovery Why this matters A research university earns its standing through the work its researchers do, not through the plan that describes it; this pillar exists to keep that work growing in scale, in ambition, and in the range of problems it takes on, while giving the University — for the first time on a continuous basis — a current account of how its research investment is actually tracking against what was promised. It also gives the University’s research leadership, for the first time, a shared account of how investment decisions across schools and institutes are actually landing, rather than a picture assembled only at each grant round or annual report.

What we’ll do 1. Diversify the University’s research income base across competitive grant funding, philanthropic support, and industry and government collaboration. 2. Expand doctoral training capacity and strengthen the candidate experience across every school. 3. Renew major research infrastructure and align priority investment with capability of recognised national significance.

Education for an Uncertain Decade Why this matters Graduates who leave [ORGANISATION] in 2031 will enter a labour market substantially reshaped from the one their degree was designed against; this pillar exists to keep the curriculum, and the judgement behind it, moving at the same pace as the world it prepares people for. It is also the pillar most exposed to the pace of external change, since the tools and expectations shaping graduate work in 2031 are, in large part, not yet invented.

The plan is the product of a year of consultation with our staff, students, alumni, partners across the cultural and research sectors, and the Council. It reflects the Council’s clear-eyed assessment of where [ORGANISATION]’s instrumental research capability sits within the national and international landscape, the trajectory it is on, and the work required to ensure that trajectory matures into a sustained national capability over the plan period. The directions set out here are deliberate. They will require —4—

coordinated effort, candid review, and a willingness to keep building on what is working rather than quietly setting it aside. I am confident in the contribution that [ORGANISATION]’s instrumental practice will make to the country, the region, and the international scholarly community across the period to 2031. The work begins now. Vice-Chancellor and President

Executive summary This plan sets out four strategic priorities that will shape the work of the [ORGANISATION] in the field of new musical instruments through to 2031. Together they describe a coherent ambition: that [ORGANISATION] will become the most consequential site for the design, study, and performance of new musical interfaces in the southern hemisphere, recognised internationally for the depth of its instrument-building research, the seriousness of its embodied scholarship, and the durability of its contribution to the practice and public life of music. The priorities are interlocking. None can be fully realised in isolation, and the plan is best read as a description of the university we are working to become over the plan period: ambitious about what an instrumental research practice can contribute, honest about the institutional foundations that contribution depends on, and recognisably [ORGANISATION].

We provide students with ample space and opportunity for personal fulfilment and professional development. [ORGANISATION] has a rich culture of student and study associations, dream teams and student teams, student societies and student clubs. This culture helps develop the soft skills that are necessary for [ORGANISATION] engineers to make an impact for a sustainable society. Nourishing this rich student culture is actively facilitated by [ORGANISATION]. The premise in doing so is that it should always be feasible to complete one’s studies at our university within the official education period of five years. Provided students spend their time wisely, we give them the opportunity to realise their ambitions over a longer period (such as a BSc in 4 years, and an MSc in 2.5 years), with the freedom to make personal choices. [ORGANISATION] endorses the importance of broad academic and personal development in a socially safe environment. [ORGANISATION] aims to be an inspiring, diverse and inclusive institution where the best researchers and the most motivated students from all over the world choose to come to develop their talents, and also an institution which is seen as an attractive organisation to professional facilitating staff. To that end, [ORGANISATION] aims to at least maintain the already very high international performance levels and to further improve in certain areas, thereby seeking a healthy balance between workload and ambition. This enables [ORGANISATION] to continue to position itself as a world-class university that stands at the centre of society, across the entire board in education, research and innovation. A university that sees the growing urgency as an important responsibility to contribute even more to the realisation of complex societal transitions.

MARINE AND MARITIME ENVIRONMENTS AND SOCIETIES We want to maintain and build upon our pre-eminence internationally for contributions to the sustainability of marine and maritime environments and societies. The marine environment is integral to the well-being of life on Earth. Covering 70% of the Earth’s surface, the marine environment is home to 95% of the Earth’s species. Humans are dependent on the oceans more than ever before – for food, oxygen, water, mineral, sustainable energy. Yet vast areas remain unexplored. Mega cities of the world are on coasts, capitalising on economic and trade benefits but impacting on, and vulnerable to, marine environments and climate change impacts. Of growing economic importance, marine and maritime industries support over 950,000 jobs in the UK. The UK has a Maritime Strategy to 2050 which supports significant investment as well as protection. In the [PLACE]-West, regional development strategy is strongly anchored in offshore renewable energy, autonomous shipping, marine cyber security and the health and well-being of both coastal and rural communities. [ORGANISATION] is pre-eminent in these matters, and more.

Priority One: Deliver excellent education and research Ensure an innovative education portfolio • Scale development of blended and experiential learning and personalised assessment. • Grow and develop the postgraduate taught offer. • Establish competitive online programmes with global reach. • Grow international student numbers and TNE programmes and partnerships to support influence. Deliver programme excellence • Predict market needs and respond to new opportunities. • Create lean and coherent portfolios grounded in research strengths. • Optimise our location and industrial links for experiential learning. • Provide opportunities for all students to engage with sustainability, not least in marine and maritime issues. Support strong research foundations and build research power • Build research power by increasing the percentage of research-active staff (as defined by the [ORGANISATION]) and growing research income. • Grow our own research talent base. • Grow a strong doctoral research community to support research intensity. • Support cross-institution interdisciplinary institutes that address global challenges.

• Develop an integrated enrolment strategy coordinating marketing, recruitment, retention, and university planning. • Transparently align resources with institutional needs and demands, prioritising student experience. • Support expansion of advancement capacity and activities. • Advance environmental sustainability initiatives that reduce our environmental footprint and model climate leadership. • Build a campus masterplan embodying accessibility and net-zero goals. • Develop long-and short-range financial plans to deliver a future in which [PLACE] continues to thrive.

Within this context, we must remain fiscally disciplined to ensure that the University remains vibrant for the next generations. Fiscal discipline requires finding efficiencies, making technology work for us, and prioritising what, and what not to do. The goal is to be agile and proactive — gathering and sharing resources collaboratively and supporting thoughtful, and inclusive decision-making through clear, evidence-informed insights. We must take a similar approach to the physical campus and capital assets. Long- and short-run planning around space utilisation, infrastructure, and campus facilities must be undertaken with environmental sustainability and accessibility in mind. Operational excellence is a foundational directive, necessary to ensure [PLACE]’s strategic vision becomes a lived reality. Designing appropriate organisational structures, streamlining processes, and aligning resources will strengthen capacity to identify emerging trends, and to swiftly capture opportunities. This can only happen when we place people at the core of this vision — building an organisation where students, faculty, staff, alumni, and community members thrive. When faculty and staff are freed from unduly complex and laborious administrative pressures, there is space for what truly matters: meaningful experiences, deep learning, and a vibrant campus environment. 26

Given the multi-year time span for this work, attention will be paid to renewing the group’s membership on an annual basis while ensuring continuity of knowledge and work.

What we’ll do 1. Move beyond first-generation reconciliation work toward structural transformation, including a renewed [ORGANISATION], sustained investment in [PLACE]-led research, and a long-term commitment to truth telling about the university’s own history. 2. Deepen engagement with the [PLACE] public service, including through expansion of executive education, renewal of long-running partnerships with policy agencies, and a sustained programme of evidence-based contribution to national decision-making. 3. Build durable partnerships with civil-society organisations, primary industries, and the cultural sector, with at least 75 active strategic partnerships of national significance by 2031.

Priority 4: A Capable and Connected Institution None of the above is achievable without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the people, the systems, and the working culture on which the university depends — and we will commit to ways of working that match the seriousness of the academic mission they support.

Why this matters The quality of an institution’s work is shaped by the quality of its internal life. Universities make their best contribution when staff have the time, the systems, and the conditions to do work of substance — and when the institution’s own practices honour the kind of careful, deliberative reasoning the academic mission depends on.

What we’ll do 1. Modernise digital infrastructure, including a renewed approach to research data, a contemporary teaching technology stack, and an institution-wide approach to artificial intelligence in education, research, and administration. 2. Renew the conditions under which institutional decisions are made and communicated, with a renewed emphasis on written briefs, working papers, and

structured discussion in place of presentation-led decision-making, so that staff time is spent on argument rather than arrangement. 3. Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds.

And this brings me to my third and final point, our vision of [ORGANISATION] as a Transformational university measured by the positive impact that we achieve for our people, students, businesses and the communities we serve. Being transformational means embedding professional practice in all our courses to drive employability and social mobility; encouraging interdisciplinary teaching and challenge-based research; developing entrepreneurs internally and externally to drive innovation and inclusive growth; facilitating a collaborative co-creation approach with industry and business focused on value realisation, embedding industry teams and professionals within the university environment; fostering lifelong connectivity with our students and expanding our international collaborations. But most of all, this means that we will need to think and act differently, beyond the conventional boundaries of today, as we create a more agile and adaptive university, a learning organisation for the future, powered by digital innovation.

“This means that we will need to think and act differently, beyond the conventional boundaries of today.” Perhaps the best example of the transformational model we have in mind is the new [PLACE] Health Services Hub that we will establish on campus within the B-IQ, to provide integrated care for all our students and the community and drive health tech innovations. A Hub that brings together cutting-edge research in precision healthcare and digital health, clinical training and clinical trials, with embedded NHS services, tech companies and expert teams from partner organisations. A ‘living lab’, in fact, that will bring together our diverse disciplines and teams to advance both education and research by prototyping and proofing new healthcare solutions and technologies to address the unprecedented challenges to health inequity and access to care. A new model of university for a changing world. This is our grand challenge at [ORGANISATION]. Bring it on.

Our focus We are dedicated to achieving success across various impact areas that directly tackle both local and national critical challenges. These challenges encompass critical issues such as technological advancements, shifting geopolitics, inequality and inequity, and climate change. We aim to make a unique and transformative contribution to tackle these critical issues which have informed our outward-facing activities:

• We will make a direct and significant contribution to innovation-led growth and ensuring we have the skills and knowledge to drive growth in emerging sectors. We acknowledge the rapid advancements in technology and their transformative effects on industries, economies and future ways of working.

• We will put ourselves at the heart of decision-making, using our knowledge and expertise to ensure a good deal for our institution and community. As a key anchor institution, we have an important role to play in attracting investment and using our expertise and soft power to raise the profile of our region.

• We will apply our expertise and influence to tackle the major societal issues which will support sustainable growth. The fourth pressure is epistemic. The sector has drifted, over the previous decade, toward measures of academic productivity that reward throughput over the slower forms of work on which a research university’s reputation is in fact built. The applause that a university most needs is not the kind that follows a flashy opening; it is the kind that follows the eleven o’clock number — the moment, late in the run, when the audience recognises the depth of what the company has been doing all along. The Plan reorients several measures in order to honour that distinction. Read together, these four pressures ask the University to articulate its purpose with the seriousness of a production that intends a long run, rather than the seriousness of a production hoping to survive its previews. The Plan accordingly addresses the dramaturgy of the institution as well as its content: not only what the University intends to do, but how it intends to stage the doing, in a register that the country can recognise and return to.

What we will become By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a national university recognised — within the country and in its region — as an institution that has earned its standing ovation. The University will have produced, across the run of this Plan, a set of structural commitments and visible moments that the country recognises as the University’s own work, performed in the University’s own voice. The disciplines will have been cast with care, the ensemble numbers rehearsed, the eleven o’clock numbers delivered. The production will, by 2031, be ready for its next chapter — not as a closing curtain but as the company moving into a second long-running season, on the same stage, for the same audience, with the same seriousness and a deeper repertoire.

Ambition: [ORGANISATION] will be at the international forefront when it comes to knowledge and competence about and for the Artic and High [PLACE]. We will be at the forefront of understanding natural and societal changes in the [PLACE] and the High [PLACE], and the effects of these. We will be an attractive place to study that utilises and values the closeness between disciplines, people and practice. We will translate challenges and opportunities in the High [PLACE] into research questions and explore them in collaboration.

2. The major societal challenges Major societal challenges covering climate and environment, food security, demography and health show that modern society is vulnerable. These challenges demonstrate that global interaction, democracy and mutual trust between people are important. Society needs academic environments that can develop research questions and methods aimed at providing the basis for challenging decision-making processes in the short and long term. Our academic breadth and closeness to nature and society make [ORGANISATION] uniquely suited to contribute knowledge and competence to transformation and adaptation processes and future-oriented solutions across disciplines, trade and industry and civil society. Ambition: [ORGANISATION] will contribute to developing innovative, democratic and sustainable solutions for major societal challenges. We will take responsibility for basic research in our disciplines and contribute to global knowledge production. We will take special responsibility for knowledge and competence needed for environmentally, socially and economically sustainable development. We will share and make available our research and education and facilitate innovation and co-creation internally and with the wider community. Students and staff at [ORGANISATION] will be characterised by their ability to think critically, gain a head start on ideas and dare to challenge established practices.

Oversight and review How this plan was developed This plan is the product of extended consultation across the [ORGANISATION] community. Over the course of 2025, the executive convened a series of facilitated workshops with academic staff, professional staff, students, alumni, and partner organisations across government, industry, and the cultural sector. The directions set out here reflect the convergence of those deliberations and have been considered and endorsed by Council through its established governance arrangements.

Accountability Council holds responsibility for oversight of this plan. The Vice-Chancellor and the executive are accountable to Council for its delivery, and each strategic priority has a designated executive sponsor with operational responsibility for its implementation. The plan will be reported on annually, both to Council and to the broader university community. The annual report will describe progress against each success measure and will be published openly on the university’s website. Reporting will be candid about what has not yet been achieved as well as what has. A mid-period review will be conducted in late 2028 by an independent panel commissioned by Council. The review will assess progress, recommend adjustments where required, and be considered by Council before any material changes are implemented through the executive.

Looking ahead The decade to 2031 will demand much of [PLACE] and of the institutions on which the country relies. [ORGANISATION] will meet that demand with the seriousness and clarity the moment requires — through the sustained effort of every member of the [ORGANISATION] community, and through the contribution it enables [ORGANISATION] to continue to make to the country and the region. The work begins now.

Fundamental rights and human rights in complex relations of power In the present day, power is more than state authority – it is also exerted by supranational bodies and powerful private stakeholders at several levels and in overlapping areas; sometimes in a fragmented, sometimes in a coordinated, and sometimes in a mutually competitive way. Regulatory and prohibitive tendencies as well as surveillance on the part of the state have increased, but today it is often argued that the fundamental freedoms of certain groups need to be restricted in order to protect the human rights of others, and the state tends to cooperate with international organisations, supranational bodies and other states in this respect. There are corporations that have reached a position of economic power that enables them to dictate their terms to staff, competitors and states alike. Search engines and social media have gathered enormous quantities of data that represent power in the form of knowledge, to which all of us are willing, though unofficial, contributors. Under these conditions, it is necessary for all legal disciplines to reconsider the issue of protecting fundamental and human rights. This key research area is designed to meet these challenges.

text:
Priority 1: Research That Meets the Moment The defining feature of [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been its proximity to the questions that matter for [PLACE] and the wider world. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — focusing investment on mission-aligned priorities, expanding our cross-disciplinary capability, and growing the research income on which the university’s future depends.

Our position A national university is not the sum of its grants and rankings; it is the standing capacity of a country to ask the questions only its national university is positioned to ask. That capacity has to be maintained, and it has to be renewed.

Our actions • Concentrate investment in a small number of flagship research programs of international standing, each addressing a problem of clear national significance and each connected to teaching at the postgraduate and research-training level. • Renew the university’s cross-disciplinary research capability — with particular emphasis on the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities and social sciences — through shared infrastructure, shared platforms, and shared methodological practice. • Strengthen the institutional supports for research integrity, research data, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence in research, ensuring that [ORGANISATION]’s research practice continues to set the standard for the sector.

Priority 2: Education for a Connected Continent The world our students will work in is being remade. Our educational programs will be redesigned around the dispositions and knowledges that will matter most over the coming decades — with particular attention to inquiry, judgement, plurality of knowledges, and the capacity for substantive engagement across disciplines under conditions of uncertainty.

Our position Education at a national university is not a transaction; it is a decade-long act of trust between the institution and the people who choose to study with us. That trust has to be earned in the design of our programs, the quality of our teaching, and the seriousness with which we treat the question of what our graduates will be ready for.

Where we work off our island, whether on the mainland or in other countries, we seek to bring our Tasmanian commitments and character to serve the communities in those places. The nature of our place brings great strengths and challenges. There is a deep commitment to environmental sustainability amongst many people here. In many areas, we lead the world. The remarkable natural qualities of [PLACE] and the deep desire to protect them meant this was the first place in the world where the Green political movement began. It has seen 50.4% of our land protected, much of it as World Heritage area. We are one of the few jurisdictions in the world with a net zero carbon economy powered by nearly 100% renewable energy. We have strong communities, each deeply connected to their place. While [PLACE] is an island, distances still divide us and each part is unique, with different social, cultural and economic challenges. It makes us a place of places. We need to care about each part, not just the whole. People want to be a part of and contribute to each of these communities. People’s passion for their place sometimes meets with widely varied values and visions of the future, which can divide us deeply. The value of a university to build capacity within the Tasmanian community to engage respectfully and constructively is central to a flourishing future of our island.

While we have strong communities, they are also small. Size can be an advantage but also a challenge. With little more than 500,000 people and a rapidly ageing population, finding the resources and the expertise to do all that [PLACE] needs from that population alone, not least in higher education, can be hard. Although we are small and often understated, [PLACE] does have a remarkable record of making globally distinctive contributions across the arts, the sciences, policy, and commerce. We are quietly proud of our part in that story, and we aspire to contribute much more to that record.

How we developed this plan This Plan was developed over fourteen months through a process of facilitated consultation across staff, students, alumni, partners, the [PERSON] Family Trust, and the country’s principal [PERSON] scholars. The [PERSON] Family Trust contributed substantively to the working group’s deliberations about the centenary programme and to the preservation arrangements for the archive. The working group also consulted with the curators of the Questacon [PERSON] exhibition (2013) and with the producers of the 2014 ABC documentary series in order to draw on the existing public-facing scholarship. The framing language of the Plan — “the [PERSON] disposition”, “the patient examination of the half-baked”, “the tartan paint line item” — emerged from the consultation rather than being imposed at the outset. Where the language has been retained, it is because participants in the working group returned to it spontaneously across multiple rounds.

Chancellor remains accountable to Council for delivery. Within that frame, three governance moves give the Plan effective traction. First, a [PERSON] Centenary Standing Committee, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting quarterly to Council, takes responsibility for the indicator set across all four priorities and for ensuring that the centenary year in 2031 finds the University in the institutional condition the tradition warrants. Second, an Accountability and Review schedule, published annually, sets out which indicators are due for full reporting in which quarter, with no indicator permitted to slip beyond the next quarterly review cycle. Third, Council’s Audit and Risk Committee will, from 2027, treat indicator slippage on the same footing as financial sustainability. Annual reporting against the Plan will be published in full, including instances of indicator slippage, elements of the Plan that have not progressed at the pace this document anticipated, and any element of the [PERSON] Centenary Programme that has been reprioritised or deferred. The reporting will not be selective.

This reset provides us with an exciting opportunity to reflect and refocus, and to ensure that, across the organisation, we are aligned to delivering against our Strategic Framework by empowering our students and staff through the opportunities we create, with the region we are part of being at the heart of what we do. The fundamental principles around our Strategic Framework reset are based on feedback from colleagues around the institution. From this feedback, it is clear we need to simplify the content of our Framework and reposition it to make it accessible and relevant to all, provide greater clarity on what we need to be doing to be successful, and capitalise on our strengths to enable us to meet the challenges and opportunities of the future.

A key element of our Strategic Framework reset is to ensure its accessibility and relevance to all staff, making sure that our strategic ambitions can be aligned to individual and team contributions and performance throughout the organisation. This image sets out the key elements which comprise our simplified representation of our Strategic Framework’s content.

What we do and how we do it through to 2030 is shaped by our Pillars, which set out what we will succeed at to fulfil our overarching Purpose and ensure the University succeeds for its students, staff and region. When our Strategic Framework was launched in 2018, there were three Pillars. GLOBAL ENGAGEMENT We will create and support opportunities for our students and staff to become globally engaged, working together with our partners to build a more sustainable world for current and future generations. Our approach to global engagement is founded on a commitment to work and deliver in partnership, valuing our multi-lingual and multicultural foundations to support our city, our regions, and our global partners.

OUR PRIORITIES A global experience We will provide a globally influenced experience for students by developing and maintaining a curriculum that reflects international issues and perspectives, increasing our international student population through a strategic, evidence-informed approach. We will ensure a global experience for all graduates through transnational education and student mobility, through which we will grow a global community that raises [PLACE]’s reputation and improves our global brand and visibility. We will promote global staff and student mobility, collaboration, and scholarship. We will create opportunities for staff and students to undertake world-class research and innovation to build the knowledge and solutions required to support society and deliver global sustainable development.

Sustainable global partnerships We will ensure our global activities are more focused and resilient, investing in our people and our strategic partnerships to realise our shared priorities, though improved communication and co-design. We will work with our global partners, Global [PLACE] and align with UK and [PLACE] Government international strategies to increase relevance and impact. We will identify and develop collaborative partnerships that will contribute to the delivery of the University’s Mission and Vision and will expand the footprint and influence of the University world-wide. A diverse and sustainable portfolio of partnerships will be strategically important to the University; this will include research, transnational education, and student and staff exchanges that will enrich experience.

Our communities We will strengthen our relationship with communities throughout [PLACE] by ensuring that our activities are relevant and recognisable to people living in the region, working with local groups and stakeholders in a collective initiative to deliver social and economic transformation. We will continue to grow our commitment to [PLACE] culture and the Arts through our teaching and research and our Arts and Innovation centre, Pontio.

ECONOMIC, SOCIAL AND CIVIC IMPACT Supporting a prosperous [PLACE], we envisage an innovation crescent, stretching from the [PLACE] Republic to the Northern powerhouse of [PLACE] West [PLACE] with the University at its heart, driving a place-based innovation agenda. We will support a wealth of civic mission activities – regionally, nationally, and internationally – and recognise these as a fundamental aspect of our core activities.

OUR PRIORITIES Supporting business We will play a lead role in the economic growth of [PLACE] and the UK, influencing and supporting key industrial sectors and their supply chains. We will focus on sectors of regional significance and those with emerging potential for growth, such as health and low carbon energy, working in partnership with public and private organisations to promote resilience and sustainability. We will build on the success of M-Sparc, our Science Park, to support our aspiration for greater employability, start-up, and commercialisation across [PLACE]. We will specifically seek to play a lead role in the growth of a vibrant health and life sciences sector across the region through the development of research in the [PLACE] [ORGANISATION].

Regional skills We will support regional workforce development through our undergraduate and postgraduate provision and the upskilling of the existing workforce through our Continuing Professional Development and professional qualifications programmes. We will lead a shared vision across the education sector in [PLACE] to bridge across statutory, further, and higher education boundaries and provide an alternative offer to established education and training routes through the development of pathways to meet regional skills needs.

Supporting early-career researchers is essential for a successful academic career. Training programmes in leadership and project management will be developed as a priority via online course materials, podcasts and more traditional forms of training. These will take place on the basis of a systematic satisfaction and needs analysis by users in order to strengthen coaching for researchers and to make optimal use of people and resources. The pathways also focus on career development and promoting non-academic career prospects. Moreover, we cannot accept the growing external pressure on unfettered research. Therefore, with training and a clearly agreed framework, we make our researchers resilient to attacks on academic freedom. Indeed, a healthy, competitive research culture goes hand in hand with a principled research environment and an appreciative human resources policy. Drawing on You Are Not Alone (YANA), the framework that ensures an integrated, coordinated and transparent approach to transgressive behaviour, we are pursuing our policy on welfare and transgressive behaviour within the organisation. These elements are widely supported and enjoy the participation of all [ORGANISATION] affiliates and stakeholders, resulting in a global reputation as a leading Urban Engaged university. Community of caring

46% of students screen positive for the criteria of one or more mental health problems. Among these students, about 5% experience no impact, 25% little to mild impact and 10% mild to moderate impact on daily life. 5% of students belong to a critical group, who have many mental health problems and experience high impact. As an Urban Engaged University, we recognise that big city living is often associated with lower socioeconomic status, which can also bring additional welfare challenges for our students. Investing in social connectedness is the best way to prevent impaired mental wellbeing in students. Our 'community of caring' includes a well-thought-out VUBuddy system and active alumni involvement. A more appropriate study progress policy with additional instruction and guidance for students will also be embedded in GSP 5. In doing so, [ORGANISATION] is putting extra effort into mandatory remediation, special measures for advancement within a programme and changes in study progress monitoring.

Strategic priorities The four priorities below structure the work of the plan period. Each is presented with a short premise, the transformation initiatives we will pursue, and the indicators by which we will track our progress.

From and to The plan represents a deliberate shift in the university’s posture across several dimensions. The transitions below are illustrative rather than exhaustive, and run through each of the priority areas that follow. From

Priority 1: Research Excellence and National Impact [ORGANISATION]’s research has always taken its character from the questions that matter for [PLACE] and the wider world. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — focusing investment on mission-aligned priorities, expanding our cross-disciplinary capability, and growing the research income on which the university’s future depends.

Why this matters A national university is judged in the long run by the substance of the research it produces and the difference that research makes to the country it serves. The decade ahead will reward institutions that concentrate their effort, sustain their depth, and remain honest about where they can lead.

2. Renew the university’s cross-disciplinary research capability, with a particular focus on the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities and social sciences, and the questions that sit between them. 3. Grow Category 1 and competitive research income substantially over the plan period, including through opportunities arising from successive [PLACE] research and capability instruments.

Priority 2: Education for the Decades Ahead The world our students will work in is being remade. Our educational programs will be redesigned around the dispositions, knowledges, and forms of inquiry that will matter most over the coming decades — with particular attention to critical perspectives, plurality of knowledges, and the capacity for sustained reasoning under uncertainty.

This is the environment this plan answers. Not a single new pressure, but the accumulation of many small ones, each asking the University to be more certain, earlier, and for longer, about the trajectories it is prepared to back. [ORGANISATION]’s setting sharpens the point rather than softening it. A university that draws its staff, students, and partners from across a single region carries a longer institutional memory of the commitments it has made there than a larger, more transient institution might; a trajectory backed badly is not easily forgotten by the people around it. Place, in that sense, is not a backdrop to this plan but a discipline on it — the University answers, over the decade ahead, to the same community it commits to, and a commitment that does not hold up under evidence will be noticed close to home before it is noticed anywhere else.

Where we are headed By 2031, no commitment [ORGANISATION] makes will outlive the evidence that justified it. This is a narrower ambition than it first sounds, and a more demanding one. It does not mean the University will commit to less, or more slowly. It means that whatever the University commits to — an appointment, an admitted cohort, a partnership, a continuing career — will carry a live account of the trajectory behind it, refreshed on a published schedule rather than assumed to still hold. A university that can show, at any point across the life of a commitment, the evidence that still justifies it, is a university whose confidence in its own decisions can be checked rather than simply taken on faith. That is the institution this plan builds toward. Reaching it means treating evidence of trajectory as infrastructure rather than paperwork: something built once, resourced properly, and maintained on a schedule the University publishes and keeps to, in the same way it maintains any other system its people and partners rely on.

Inclusive excellence and leadership in research and innovation allow us to have the broadest and deepest impact in scholarship and on society. We will continue to lead in research funding, global rankings and international recognition of our academic excellence, and through our successes in innovation and entrepreneurship.

We will provide all members of our scholarly community with the necessary supports they need to be successful and competitive. We will create and refine tools, policies, best practices and procedures that advance research and innovation, ensuring the highest standards of ethics, integrity and accountability.

Our research and teaching missions are inextricably linked. Research-informed teaching innovations, standards and practices enhance the entire educational mission and position the university as the top destination for future students, postdoctoral fellows, researchers and innovators. Our innovation and entrepreneurship community provides mentorship, expertise, space and networks for all stages of the innovation journey for students and faculty. These programs not only strengthen existing areas of excellence and develop new ones, but they also increase synergies between teaching and research.

Collaborations and partnerships with communities, governments, NGOs, industry and within the university itself allow us to leverage complementary research strengths, which produce unique capabilities that foster learning, promote critical inquiry and accelerate discovery. The university plays an important role in addressing local and global challenges by engaging with communities as partners and by advancing solutions that are sustainable, equitable and serve the needs of those communities.

Our researchers are studying the factors that influence quality of life in communities, as well as developing partnerships and ethically engaging in [PLACE] and Inuit-related research to learn from and with community members. Our researchers are also exploring how to strengthen democratic and civil institutions by making governance more inclusive, participatory, respectful of diversity, and responsive to issues of autonomy, equity and social justice.

priorities already in motion, not to issue them from the centre. Direction does not disappear — it is exercised earlier, in the anticipatory work, and distributed more widely — but the plan’s own role becomes ratification: the orderly, accountable acknowledgement that a priority has emerged, been tested, and earned a place in the institution’s record.

Our actions. 1. Redefine the strategic plan, in the University’s governance instruments, as a ratifying record rather than a directive one: inclusion in the plan certifies that a priority has emerged and been pursued, and confers resource, but does not itself originate the priority. 2. Establish a published test for ratification — evidence that a priority has been enacted somewhere in the institution for at least one full cycle — and apply it without exception, so that no priority is written into the plan on the strength of intention alone. 3. Devolve the authority to begin pursuing an emerging priority to schools and portfolios, ahead of ratification, under a standing mandate that treats early, evidenced action as the ordinary way priorities enter the University rather than as an irregularity to be corrected. Our targets. • From 2028, every priority in the live plan will carry a public ratification record showing where and for how long it was enacted before it was included, and no priority will appear in the plan without one.

• By 2030, no strategic priority will be originated by the planning process itself; the University will be able to trace every priority in its plan to an emergence that preceded its ratification, and will publish any case it cannot. • Throughout the plan period, the University will maintain a published register of priorities it began pursuing before ratification, with no entry removed to tidy the record, so that the institution’s anticipatory action remains auditable.

• Median time between an asset becoming unavailable and its replacement or repair falls by at least half against the pre-Register baseline. • Register update compliance, a steward’s entry reviewed within its due cycle, holds above 95% every year from 2028 onward. • Every newly named steward completes induction within one month of appearing on the Register, with no backlog carried past a single reporting quarter.

Capability Through Clear Custodianship Why this matters Shared research equipment and actively maintained datasets currently rely on inherited knowledge of who looks after what, passed on informally when a custodian moves between labs or leaves the University altogether. Formal, attested custodianship protects research capability directly: an instrument that is calibrated on schedule and handed on cleanly serves every project that depends on it, not just the one that happened to be running when it was last checked. The University’s research strategy already depends, in practice, on this kind of custody working quietly in the background; this priority simply makes that dependency visible, named, and reviewable rather than trusting it to survive the next round of staff turnover by luck.

1. Assign a named custodian to every item of shared research equipment and every actively maintained dataset, published on the research-infrastructure register alongside the Stewardship Register. 2. Require an annual custodianship attestation, renewed or formally reassigned, with a documented succession protocol triggered the moment a custodian departs. 3. Route every custodian-reported fault directly into the relevant lab’s maintenance queue, closing the loop between a report and its resolution. 4. Publish a lightweight custodianship handbook for each equipment category — calibration cadence, fault-reporting steps, succession checklist — so a new custodian inherits a procedure, not just a name. How we’ll know • 100% of shared research equipment carries an active, attested custodian by 2029. • Average custodian tenure at handover exceeds eighteen months, with a documented successor named within a fortnight of any departure. • Equipment fault-to-resolution time falls year-on-year for the remainder of the plan. • Every equipment category carries a published handbook, reviewed at each custodianship handover without exception.
