Education That Shapes the Future Why this matters. The graduates who pass through [ORGANISATION] during the plan period will work for forty to fifty years across fields whose shape we cannot fully predict. The strongest preparation we can offer is not a fixed body of knowledge — though knowledge matters — but the dispositions and forms of practice that allow a person to keep learning, keep contributing, and keep adapting through long working lives in unsettled fields. Education at [ORGANISATION] should equip graduates to do that work well. What we’ll do. 1. Renew the undergraduate curriculum around durable capabilities and forms of practice, including studio-style and ensemble learning formats in which students rehearse the moves of inquiry and collaboration alongside academic content, rather than acquiring content in isolation from the work it is meant to support. 2. Deepen the integration of research into education at every level, so that students at every stage encounter live questions, contribute to ongoing work, and develop the judgement that comes from sustained engagement with real problems. 3. Strengthen postgraduate and professional education as a coherent program of study, including renewed Masters offerings, expanded micro-credentialing in areas of national capability need, and professional pathways that complement the HDR program rather than competing with it. How we’ll know. • Sustained improvement in graduate satisfaction, employability, and destinations, particularly in fields of national capability need. — 10 —

• Growth in postgraduate and professional education enrolments by approximately 25–35% over the plan period, with a corresponding diversification of the student body. • Doubling of the proportion of [PLACE] students across the university by 2031, supported by renewed pathways and sustained institutional commitment.

text: We will strengthen cooperation with the world of work so that it permeates the entire educational trajectory, such as the preparation and evaluation of study programmes, internships and mentoring during studies (e.g. consistent promotion and cooperation with selected [PLACE] and foreign institutions, connecting teachers and professionals), and specialised educational offerings, as well as the employment of graduates. • We will strive to establish a clinical school as a space for developing the competencies of future teachers as part of their undergraduate training and pedagogical research at teacher training faculties. • We will create a modern educational environment that combines the best elements of traditional teaching with innovative AI tools and supports personalised learning, immediate feedback, simulations, and the practical application of theoretical knowledge, as well as an understanding of students’ individual needs. Roadmap The plan will be delivered in four overlapping phases across the period to 2031. The phases are sequential in emphasis but not in start — each priority will have activity under way from the first year of the plan.

Foundation (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each priority will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in flagship research programs, in educational redesign, and in the digital and physical infrastructure that supports them — will commence.

Acceleration (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

Consolidation (2029-2030) Through 2029 and 2030, the focus will shift from build to sustained operational delivery. Programs will be tuned for outcomes; partnerships will deepen; success measures will be tracked publicly and acted on. The cultural and structural changes initiated in earlier phases will be expected to be visible in the lived experience of staff and students.

Legacy (2031) In 2031 we will assess what the plan has delivered, recalibrate where outcomes have not been met, and prepare the strategic direction for the period beyond. The 2031 review will be conducted with the same depth of consultation that produced this plan, and the lessons learned across the period will be carried into the next.

How we developed this plan This plan is the product of an extended period of structured consultation across the [ORGANISATION] community. Over the course of 2025, the executive convened a sequence of facilitated workshops with academic and professional staff, undergraduate and postgraduate students, alumni, and external partners, including representatives of the [PLACE] public service, industry, the cultural sector, and [PLACE] communities with long-standing relationships to the university.

We serve our communities, [PLACE] and around the globe, working with partners who share our values and passion for positive impact to create a better world. VISION We aspire to be a transformative power. We will be renowned for the exceptional quality of our education and the experiences of our students, our world-class research with far-reaching impact, and the highest standards in [PLACE] in our progressive academic health system. [ORGANISATION] will respond to the needs of a rapidly changing world and shape its future, becoming: • a destination of choice for students • a continuously accelerating powerhouse of impactful research • an employer of choice for our staff • a provider of choice for people engaged with our health enterprise • a community where everyone is valued, included and respected • more deeply aligned with [PLACE] peoples • a nexus for partnership and innovation in [PLACE] and around the world • a place of pride for graduates and alumni • agile in response to the rapidly changing national and global landscape • enduring and sustainable.

A gathering of students and staff with a shared vision of what it means to belong to a university that serves the nation and the world. Our remarkable students and dedicated staff are the lifeblood of an open, ethical and diverse [ORGANISATION] community: • our students and alumni will realise the benefits of both their education and broader experiences at [ORGANISATION] throughout their lives so they might achieve their hopes, dreams and aspirations • for staff, [PLACE] will be a place of professional achievement, satisfaction and belonging in the service of advancing the University • those receiving treatment and support in our health services will find healing, learning and discovery at the heart of all that we do. Every student, along with every staff member, should find their lives enriched and enhanced by the opportunities they find at this University at the same time as their studies and work enrich the University’s standing and the world we serve.

[PLACE] communities and scholars, the [PLACE] public service, and members of the international scholarly community all contributed. The process included a series of facilitated workshops, written submissions, partner roundtables, and focused engagements with under-represented voices within the university community. A standing reference group reviewed successive drafts; the academic and professional communities of the university tested the emerging directions; Council deliberated on the plan in successive meetings before adopting the final document. The plan that follows is the product of that process, and the directions it sets out are informed by the evidence and judgement of the many people who shaped it.

Looking ahead The decade ahead will not be a quiet one. [PLACE] universities are operating in a period in which the public, the government, and the international community all expect more substantive contributions than they have for some time, and in which the conditions of that contribution are themselves in flux. [ORGANISATION] is well placed to meet that moment. We are a national university with a particular role, a deep research culture, and a long-standing relationship with the public life of the country. The plan set out here is a description of how we intend to play that role across the period to 2031, and how we will remain open to the evidence of how the decade actually unfolds. The work that follows is the work of an institution that knows what it is for and intends to do that work well. It will require sustained effort across the university and across the decade. The contribution that [ORGANISATION] will make to [PLACE], the region, and the world over the period ahead will be the measure of how well we do it.

text:
A connected university To increase both our scientific and societal impact, we will connect with partners and focus on select academic, industrial and triple-helix partnerships in the Brainport region, at national and international level. Key to every aspect of this vision are the people that together create TU/e, its community and its outstanding achievements. TU [PLACE] is a human-centered employer, providing opportunities for talent – in both scientific and professional staff – for personal development and to engage the challenges of tomorrow together.

The Institutional Plan 2020-2025 serves as the implementation of [ORGANISATION] towards 2025. It is an inspiring, enthusing and framing document for the entire TU/e. Its implementation aims to ensure a lively, transparent and cohesive process. In addition, each department, service and individual is invited to consider how our mission, vision and strategic goals can be translated into actions within their own practice. The strategic cycle enables a ‘rolling agenda’, in which we can continuously improve and update the direction and speed of our strategy implementation. We will evaluate at least on an annual basis whether the ambitions are realistic in view of our workload, budget and relevant external developments. Given the pace of global developments, this evaluation will include trend watching and scenario planning. In our expedition towards [ORGANISATION], we travelled together with our staff, students, external experts, and everyone otherwise involved with our university. Since people always have been and always will be the heart and soul of TU/e, we invite everyone to actively take part in shaping our education, our research, our impact and our organisation toward 2030.

text:
Our digital transformation will empower every student and colleague with the skills and adaptability needed to thrive now and in the future in this increasingly digitally enabled world. We will create a seamless, personalised digital environment that enhances the student experience and supports both academic and operational excellence.

The [PLACE] Met campus has transformed over the past decade, and we believe it is among the very best in the UK. Its development is an ongoing priority, and we will remain proactive in our approach to investing in the physical foundations that enable excellent education and research, ensuring the estate is efficient, flexible, and ready for the future.

We recognise that AI’s central role in much of today’s digital innovation presents both opportunity and challenge. Our approach will be practical and ethical, improving pedagogy in support of Digitally Enhanced Learning, Teaching and Assessment (DELTA), research practice and navigation of services, while building digital literacy for students, researchers and colleagues and narrowing the digital divide.

We will expand innovations including mobile-first and hyflex learning environments, along with ethically embedded digital services. We will automate key steps in the student journey and use data-driven decision making to provide support at the right time, including increasingly personalised messaging. We will also unify and simplify the student-facing experience, making guidance, services, and learning tools intuitive, equitable, and available on the go. Supporting academic and operational excellence, we will continue to invest in resilient, accessible and forward-looking digital infrastructure, ensuring our community benefits from the latest technologies and practices. We will provide high-performance computing and secure research data environments that enable responsible access to sensitive data, accelerate discovery, collaboration, and interdisciplinary work. Alongside this, we will strengthen the reliability, agility and cybersecurity of our systems. We will also integrate digital in the development of the University’s estate, embracing smart campus technologies to support everything from space optimisation to sustainability.

text: Develop the residential experience to ensure that it serves as an intellectual and artistic incubator for educational excellence. The College and Conservatory create connected learning by developing a learning environment that prioritises face-to-face interpersonal engagement and seamlessly connects a range of opportunities and supports through the residential experience. Campus life serves as a workshop to cultivate the skills and dispositions that enable students to become lifelong learners and transformative leaders in whatever fields they pursue and communities in which they participate. Both the residential campus and [PLACE]’s location offer unique resources for creating this space for learning that remains a lifelong touchstone for [PLACE] alumni. On campus, our Allen Memorial Art Museum; Science Centre; Adam Joseph Lewis Centre for Environmental Studies; Conservatory buildings and performance spaces, including Finney Chapel and Hall Auditorium; along with other classroom buildings, libraries, and student residences, provide spaces for teaching and learning. But, equally important, these are spaces where students, faculty, and staff meet, study, work together on research projects and other collaborative pursuits, listen to concerts and lectures, develop entrepreneurial ideas, and socialise. All of these activities are central to [PLACE]’s philosophy of active engagement and pursuing excellence in an inclusive educational environment. The personal connections that develop in a residential college community, and only in such a community, are also vitally important at [PLACE]. The residential college experience—connecting the curricular, co-curricular, and extracurricular— becomes a critical laboratory for developing the skills in communication and interaction, reflection and engagement, tolerance and openness, and advocacy and dissent that sustain a dynamic intellectual environment. Looking forward, we need to integrate the learning opportunities of our residential experience more fully with those of our core academic programs. One way to approach such integration is to develop a culture of active engagement on our campus.

Our aspiration By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a university recognised — nationally and internationally — as a steward of the conditions under which the deepest forms of inquiry and education are possible. The University will operate within a published institutional carrying capacity. Its disciplines will be tended as a polyculture rather than ranked as a monoculture. Its partnerships will be measured by their reciprocity, not their volume. Its calendar will include fallow weeks in which the institution practises the kinds of pause that —8—

intergenerational scholarship requires. Its capital footprint will be smaller than it is today and its intellectual footprint deeper. Above all, the University will have demonstrated — not asserted — that the long maintain is itself a serious form of national contribution, and one that no other institution in the country is better placed to model.

Our priorities The four priorities below describe how the reorientation of the plan will be made operational. Each priority is introduced by the question it addresses, followed by the structural commitments through which the University will give the priority real purchase. Before the priorities are unpacked in detail, the table below names the shifts in framing that underpin them as a whole. From

Soil Stewardship and the Long Maintain Why this matters. The intellectual, financial, ecological, and relational substrates that have sustained [ORGANISATION] since 1946 cannot be assumed. They are produced — and depleted — by the choices the University makes about what it builds, what it lets go, and what it tends across long cycles. The reorientation this plan describes begins with the soil. Without an honest account of the conditions that make scholarship possible, every subsequent priority risks being read as a slogan. The starting work, accordingly, is the maintenance and improvement of the substrates themselves, treated as a serious institutional discipline rather than the residue left over after planning. What we’ll do. —9—

text:
Strategic pillars Pillar 1: Discovery for the Nation [ORGANISATION]’s research has always been distinguished by purpose, scale, and proximity to the questions that matter for [PLACE]. Over the plan period we will sharpen that distinctiveness — concentrating investment in mission-aligned research priorities, expanding cross-disciplinary capability, and growing our research income through programs that deliver national impact.

Transformation initiatives • Strengthen mission-aligned research in critical and emerging technologies, with sustained investment in three to five flagship programs. • Build the country’s most ambitious cross-disciplinary research initiatives at the intersections of computing, the life sciences, and the humanities. • Grow Category 1 research income through nationally significant programs, with a particular focus on opportunities arising from the National Reconstruction Fund and successor instruments. • Expand sovereign research infrastructure — high-performance computing, secure facilities, and specialist instruments — across the campus and partner sites.

Pillar 2: Education for a Changing World The world our students will work in is being remade. Our educational programs will be redesigned around the dispositions and capabilities that will matter most over the coming decades: deep disciplinary judgement, comfort with technical complexity, and the capacity for inquiry under uncertainty.

Transformation initiatives • Renew the undergraduate experience around inquiry, judgement, and futures literacy, with substantive curriculum redesign across all colleges by 2028. • Build new postgraduate programs in [PLACE] affairs, advanced computing, and public policy, drawing on [ORGANISATION]’s distinctive depth in each area. • Embed work-integrated and placement-based learning across all faculties, with particular emphasis on partnerships with the federal public service and key industries. • Lift HDR completions and reduce mean time-to-completion through redesigned candidature support and renewed supervisory frameworks.

Pillar 3: Engagement and Reconciliation Universities flourish through their relationships with the communities they serve. Over the plan period we will deepen our partnership with [PLACE] communities, sustain our engagement with the federal public service, and build durable industry partnerships in the sectors that matter most for [PLACE]’s future.

text: Climate change is proceeding apace. The growing threat to the ability of the world to sustain a growing population can only be countered through joint global action towards behavioural change and more environmentally friendly technologies. The impact of climate change – temperature increases, natural disasters, thawing permafrost, rising sea levels – will not only be felt by coastal cities. Consequences such as droughts, famines and biodiversity loss pose a threat to global food systems and food security in both poor and prosperous regions alike – developments that jeopardise peace and security. We are witnessing the development of new technologies for r­ enewable energy production and storage and energy-­ efficient systems for both household and industrial use. These technologies will provide a bridge to a low-emission or emission-free future. It is only possible to achieve a sustainable resource economy – one that also takes the growth and well­-being of developing and emerging econ­ omies into account – through internationally recognised cooperation in research and training that cuts across borders. The population is ageing. Birth rates are low in many industrialised nations, while many people born in baby-boom years are reaching retirement age. The resulting imbalance is jeopardising the long-term stability of healthcare and social welfare systems. Meanwhile, life expectancy is increasing thanks to the progress of modern medi­cine. In order for people to live longer lives while remaining healthy, society is looking to the scientific community for solutions: prevention and treatment that is affordable and can be sustained across generations. Urbanisation is creating megacities. All across the world, there has been an increase in mobility and migration from rural regions. The drivers are population growth, coupled with a lack of economic perspectives and the impact of climate change. Growing urbanisation requires expanding the sustainable infrastructure of new megacities in a way that considers people’s needs. These areas will influence a large part of global economic growth in the future. Society is orienting itself towards a multipolar world in which education, technology and innovation will play a central role.

The third signal is the country’s collective unpreparedness. The working group has consulted with senior figures across the public service, the political class, and civil society and has come to the view that the country does not yet have a settled framework for the social, economic, and democratic consequences of the working assumption. The University considers itself uniquely placed to contribute to that framework. The fourth signal is the rate at which graduate destinations are already shifting. The early cohorts entering the workforce in 2025 and 2026 are encountering professional conditions different in kind, not merely in degree, from the conditions their immediate predecessors encountered. The working group has examined the destination data across the previous three undergraduate cohorts and has concluded that the trend is consistent with the working assumption. Read together, these four signals ask the University to articulate a posture that is structurally responsive to the moment. The posture this Plan adopts is, by deliberate institutional choice, more sharply specified than the postures of recent strategic plans. The University is acting on the working assumption, not waiting for it to be confirmed.

Our ambition By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a university that has, over the run of this Plan, structurally reshaped itself in light of the working assumption and made a substantive contribution to the country’s preparation for the conditions the working assumption describes. The University will have wound down those of its functions whose continuation is no longer defensible, cultivated the institutional and civic vocations the working group considers least automatable, and contributed visibly to the democratic shaping of the post-cognitive-labour settlement. The University will be smaller in some dimensions and larger in others. It will, by 2031, be the institution the country requires it to be in the conditions the country will, by then, be operating in.

Our actions. 1. Establish the [ORGANISATION] as the University’s primary planning instrument — a public, continuously maintained account of priorities on approach, each entry carrying the date it was first sensed, the evidence for its emergence, and its current standing between sensed and ratified. 2. Commission the [ORGANISATION] to run a standing horizon-scanning program across every school and portfolio, surfacing forming priorities to the University Executive on a monthly cadence rather than at the planning cycle’s convenience. 3. Extend the [ORGANISATION] to every operational area, so that the distance between the University’s stated priorities and its enacted ones is measured continuously and published, and so that a widening gap is treated as an early signal of a priority the plan has not yet caught. Our targets. • By 2028, every strategic priority the University adopts will appear first on the [ORGANISATION] — dated, evidenced, and public — before it appears in any other planning document, with no exception sustained for more than a single review cycle. • The [ORGANISATION] will be reviewed every quarter from 2027, and no priority will be permitted to enter a University plan without a Register entry establishing that it was sensed before it was set. • By 2031, the median interval between a priority’s first appearance on the Register and its independent confirmation as an institutional priority will exceed twelve months, demonstrating that the University routinely senses its priorities a year before it would once have declared them. —9—

Ratification, Not Direction Our position. A plan that records priorities the institution is already pursuing cannot also pretend to be the source of them. The third priority is the constitutional one: to reconceive the University’s planning authority as the power to recognise and ratify — 10 —

The University’s policies and procedures strictly prohibit all forms of discrimination, vilification, intimidation, violence, and other disrespectful or oppressive behaviours, regardless of cultural background, religion, gender, or political conviction. Where standards are not met [ORGANISATION] acts decisively to uphold these standards. From 2026, all coursework students and Higher Degree by Research (HDR) candidates will be required to complete the [ORGANISATION] Rights, Relationships and Respect online module. This mandatory training meets baseline requirements of the National Higher Education Code to Prevent and Respond to Gender‑based Violence, ensuring that all students receive foundational education on respectful relationships, consent and safety. Also from 2026, [ORGANISATION] will implement the Workplace Gender Equality Agency (WGEA) targetsetting requirements, which require large employers to select, monitor and publicly report on measurable gender equality objectives on a three‑year cycle.

Health, safety and wellbeing [ORGANISATION] promotes excellence in health and safety leadership for staff, students, visitors and contractors. The University maintains a comprehensive work health and safety management system shaped by its operational context and ensures consistent implementation across all campuses, functions and activities to support a safe and healthy working and learning environment.

Engaged Alumni [ORGANISATION] is committed to cultivating lifelong relationships with its alumni. [ORGANISATION] graduates hold influential leadership roles across [PLACE] and around the world, spanning government, business, academia and the not‑for‑profit sector. The University actively seeks to harness this collective expertise and experience to create meaningful opportunities for current students and staff through mentoring, networking and collaborative initiatives. By strengthening these enduring connections, [ORGANISATION] deepens its global community and ensures alumni remain active contributors to the University’s mission, reputation and long‑term success.

text:
Education That Shapes the Future Why this matters — A grade tells the University what a student achieved; it says very little about whether the student was in the room while achieving it. As teaching moves further across lecture theatres, tutorial rooms, and recorded delivery, the University’s ability to say who actually engaged, and when, has not kept pace with its ability to say who eventually passed. This is not a proposal to make attendance compulsory in spirit — it already is, in every unit outline that lists participation as an expectation. It is a proposal to stop treating that expectation as unenforceable simply because the University has not, until now, looked at the record it was already keeping of whether anyone met it.

What we’ll do — 1. Extend swipe-card readers to every lecture theatre and tutorial room by 2028, matching the coverage already standard in professional and research spaces. 2. Instrument the lecture-capture platform with a recurring engagement ping during recorded and livestreamed delivery, logged against the enrolled student rather than the device. 3. Link swipe-derived and ping-derived attendance to scholarship renewal and progression review, alongside — not instead of — academic performance. 4. Publish a unit-by-unit presence comparison across delivery modes, so a fully online unit and a fully in-person unit are held to the same recorded standard rather than exempted from one another. How we’ll know — —9—

• A published Presence Index for every unit of study will track the gap between enrolment and recorded appearance by 2027. • 100% of first-year units will carry a minimum recorded-attendance threshold before a final grade is released by 2029, with no standing exception carried past a single semester. • By 2031, scholarship and progression panels will receive a presence record alongside every academic transcript they review. • The cross-mode presence comparison will publish for every unit of study by 2030, with no delivery mode carrying a lower recorded-attendance threshold than another.

Executive summary [ORGANISATION] enters the plan period with a mature research capability in foresight and measurement, and with a settled conviction that its planning has, for some years, been describing the institution’s priorities a little after the institution adopted them. This Plan reorganises the University’s strategy around a single principle: that priorities emerge in practice before they can be planned, and that the proper work of a plan is to sense them, record them, recognise them, and resource the people already pursuing them. The Plan is organised around four priorities — themselves recognised rather than invented.

The four priorities are sequenced to reinforce one another. Anticipation comes first, because a plan cannot record what the institution has not learned to sense; the community is built continuously, because the capability to act ahead of the plan lives in people rather than in any register. Each priority carries its own actions and targets, set out in the body of this Plan, and each is phased across the period 2026 to 2031. The University does not regard this reorientation as an admission that planning has failed. It regards it as the form planning takes once an institution is honest about where its priorities actually come from. The sections that follow set out the environment that produced this judgement, the ambition it serves, and the mechanisms — anticipatory, continuous, and accountable — through which the University will deliver it.

We will proactively collaborate in the post-secondary education sector to make education more accessible and affordable for learners, and more rapidly responsive to emerging industry skills needs. ​ From the first query to life as an alumnus, we will provide outstanding service and support. We will ensure that every student, from every background, feels valued, empowered, and prepared for lifelong success. ​

Our curriculum offerings will be grounded in a strong set of graduate attributes and capabilities that support lifelong success, adaptability, and meaningful contribution to society. Students will be prepared for citizenship, engaged in their communities, and connected to the world.​ Throughout their academic journey, students will be supported holistically, with a strong focus on wellbeing and personal growth. ​

Sustainable Learning and Teaching Our curriculum offerings will be both relevant and sustainable. We will build upon our existing strengths to deliver teaching and learning of uncompromising quality, to equip students with the skills and knowledge to thrive. ​

Research builds upon discovery at our University. It is a shared endeavour powered by curiosity, collaboration, and a commitment to improving lives. Our researchers work closely with communities, industry, and partners to tackle the issues that matter most to our regions and the world.

Our measures of success and focus areas for Research with Impact are outlined here, while the detail on the initiatives and actions that will bring the strategy to life is contained in our supporting Research Plan. This plan will support staff and students to navigate research through clear protocols, governance frameworks, and practical implementation steps.

Through multidimensional collaborations and co-creation with stakeholders, we will unlock new opportunities for impactful innovation, knowledge exchange, and shared success. ​ Our approach will embrace diversity and belonging to ensure culturally respectful and inclusive outcomes that shape a better future.

Accountability and review The University Council retains ultimate oversight of this plan and receives the assurance architecture’s delivery-confidence reporting each quarter, alongside the narrative account each pillar lead provides in the ordinary course. The Executive is accountable for delivery against every initiative in this document and for the quarterly reallocation decisions the assurance architecture recommends, which remain decisions for the Executive to make rather than actions the system takes on its own authority. The question of whether the assurance architecture itself remains proportionate to what it oversees is not one the architecture can answer about itself. That review sits with the [ORGANISATION]’s [ORGANISATION] program, convened by Dr [PERSON], which will periodically assess whether the assurance system’s own scope, cost, and authority remain in proportion to the delivery risk it was built to manage, and report that assessment to the Council independently of the pillar it reviews.

The decade ahead The five years to 2031 will ask more of [ORGANISATION] than any single plan period has asked before — not because the ambitions in this document are larger than earlier ones, though in places they are, but because the University is asking itself to hold those ambitions to a higher standard of proof as it goes. A university that can show its work, continuously and honestly, is a university better placed to earn the trust the decade ahead will demand of it. This is the university [ORGANISATION] intends to become, and the account of how it is becoming that university will, for the first time, be available before the five years are up.

Executive summary This plan sets out five strategic priorities that will shape the work of the [ORGANISATION] through to 2031. Together they describe a coherent ambition: that [ORGANISATION] will become the country’s most consequential site for the integrated study of energies — historical, material, somatic, and planetary — and the most reliable institution for the cultivation of an energetic imagination across the disciplines on which [PLACE] public life depends.

The priorities are interlocking. None can be fully realised in isolation, and the plan is best read as a description of the university we are working to become over the plan period: attentive to the conditions on which institutional life rests, accountable for the energies it draws on and the energies it produces, and recognisably [ORGANISATION].

The remainder of this document sets out, for each priority, the transformation initiatives we will pursue and the measures by which we will track our progress. It also describes the implementation phases that will deliver the plan and the governance arrangements that will hold us accountable to the directions set out here.

transformations are reshaping the operating environment for the university, and each interacts with the others in ways that demand a coordinated institutional response. The first is the maturation of the planetary energy transition. The decade ahead will see substantial decarbonisation of the country’s energy infrastructure, the recomposition of major industrial sectors, and the renewal of the cultural and political settings within which those shifts will be undertaken. Universities sit at the intersection of those shifts — as producers of the knowledge on which the transition depends, as educators of the workforces that will deliver it, and as institutions whose own operations are themselves part of the transition.

text: 4.9.2 Thematic Areas and Key Research Areas The Faculty is undergoing a period of personnel changes. The thematic areas and key research areas below will therefore need to be reviewed in 2023. To further specify the aforementioned general objectives of the Faculty, the next few years will be characterised by basic and application-oriented research with the goal of gaining academic insights into the following broad thematic areas. The focus will be primarily on psychological processes and foundations in the context of societal change for individuals and groups, in order to gain further insights with regard to meeting the [[ORGANISATION]]. Thematic area of cognition, emotion and methods in psychology: Cognition and emotion, as well as their interactions, play a special role in almost all areas of human experience and behaviour. In order to understand these central phenomena more profoundly, laboratory experiments and neuropsychological research approaches are primarily being pursued. Moreover, methods are being developed and advanced that can provide answers to open questions concerning the neuronal biological basis and the functional principles and mechanisms of cognition and emotion. This particularly includes aspects of visual cognition and attention, their interaction with emotions for the origination of aesthetic processes, the cognitive and emotional foundations of social behaviour, their neurophysiological basis, as well as their potential role in the development, diagnosis and treatment of clinical disorders. Additional important input is being provided through methods of research synthesis, machine learning and metascientific approaches. Research in this field is often interdisciplinary and characterised by cooperation with, for instance, experts in the areas of cognitive science and neuroscience, clinical psychology and neuropsychology, as well as cognitive biology. Over the next few years, this thematic area will be expanded to include innovative application-related research. Thematic area of occupational, economic and social psychology: People have to cope with massive challenges and changes at work, in the economic world and in society. Workers face the need to adapt to new and flexible requirements at work, and a prolongation of their working lives.

[PLACE]-cutting themes of the strategy The function of the cross-cutting themes [ORGANISATION]'s strategic goals define what is to be achieved, while the cross-cutting themes determine how the strategy is to be implemented in a sustainable and coherent manner. They ensure that core values and principles are embedded in all measures. The strategic goals set the direction: they define the concrete changes needed to further develop the university. The cross-cutting themes, on the other hand, ensure coherence, quality, and lasting impact by integrating core values and principles into all actions and decisions. Strategic goals answer the question: “What do we want to achieve?”

The development of the cross-cutting themes The selection of the cross-cutting themes is based on a comprehensive analysis conducted as part of the fuTUre fit process. Particular consideration was given to insights from the first phase ("Listening"), the working group reports, and discussions during the fuTUre fit Convention. These findings revealed overarching themes essential for the effective implementation of the strategy. At the same time, recurring concerns and structural challenges emerged that play a key role in [ORGANISATION]’s strategic development. The cross-cutting themes thus reflect aspects that have crystallised as strategically relevant priorities for the entire university. They were not defined in the abstract but are directly derived from the real challenges, opportunities, and needs of the university community. By integrating these cross-cutting themes into all strategic measures, they ensure that the strategy not only sets ambitious goals but also provides clear guidelines for [ORGANISATION]’s sustainable and future-oriented development.

Customer orientation & de-bureaucratization At [ORGANISATION], we understand customers to be all persons and organisations that rely on our services, expertise, or support - both internally and externally. This includes students, researchers, staff, and collaboration partners. Customer orientation means treating each other with respect, reliability, and a strong service mindset. Within [ORGANISATION], we treat each other with respect and strive to make processes clear, efficient, and supportive. Relation to the overall strategy: 

Service chains The overarching goal is to create a seamless support for our primary processes: the customer should not notice which departments, services or teams are involved in delivering the desired support. We should make the transition from support staff to professional staff. From ‘your wish is our command’ to proactive partnerships. Collaboration is the key to success. We tackle challenges in teams by having the end in mind, not by each department optimising their own subproblem. All relevant – and only the relevant – departments in a service chain are working together. People move in and out of teams when

needed. Some chains have a more permanent character, mainly in the basic services we provide. The people in the teams are empowered and trusted to solve issues based on their professional experience. They do not need unnecessary blessings from the top.

The first ‘chain’ that will be taken up is the research life cycle. A researcher requires all kinds of support in the whole process from first idea to reaching out on research results. Additionally, other potential chains are evaluated and an ‘idea box’ will be created to allow for continuous improvement projects.

Quality of service performance In quality of service performance the goal is to create a culture where it is normal to measure quality in service performances as well in order to improve the quality of services. As was acknowledged by the NVAO in their institutional quality assurance report in 2020, for education and research we have many different means to measure and evaluate the quality of our work. However, for the administration and service processes we need to step up quality measurements to better deliver services that are needed at a higher level where desired.

Vice-Chancellor’s introduction This Strategic Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan does so through a framing the working group settled on early in the drafting process and held throughout: that an institution of [ORGANISATION]’s complexity is best understood as a production — a long-running production with an overture, character arcs, ensemble numbers, and a closing standing ovation that the institution intends to earn rather than expect. The framing is not metaphorical decoration. A long-running production has the same operational characteristics as a long-running national institution. It requires a script that the company believes in. It requires rehearsal time that the schedule must protect. It requires a producer’s discipline about which numbers are working and which are not. And it requires an honest assessment, at the end of each season, of where the production is on its run.

This Plan describes how the University will run its production over the next five years. It describes the kinds of standing-ovation moments — the showstoppers, the eleven o’clock numbers, the encores — that the institution intends to earn, and it describes the kinds of supporting work, often invisible from the stalls, that those moments require. We commend the Plan to the University community in the conviction that a national university which understands its own staging is a national university more likely to do its work well. Vice-Chancellor and President

Strategic priorities The Three-Year Horizon and the Wind-Down of Cognitive Labour Premise. The working assumption set out in the foreword has particular implications for those institutional functions whose continuation, on the working assumption, is no longer defensible. The Plan addresses those functions honestly, in the conviction that a national research university owes the staff, students, and country it serves a structured, dignified, and well-supported wind-down rather than a gradual erosion under conditions of denial. Initiatives. 1. Establish the AI Transition Office, chaired by a Deputy Vice-Chancellor and reporting directly to Council, charged with identifying institutional functions for structured wind-down and supporting the people whose work the wind-down affects. 2. Publish, by the end of 2026, an Honesty Statement on the AI Transition, addressed to current students and reviewed annually, setting out the working group’s best assessment of the conditions graduates of each degree will encounter on entering the workforce. 3. Convene a quarterly Three-Year Horizon Review, chaired by the Vice-Chancellor and attended by the Deputy Vice-Chancellors, examining the current state of the working assumption and the University’s structural response. Measures. 1. By the end of 2026, the Honesty Statement on the AI Transition will have been published and made accessible to every current student of the University. 2. By 2029, the AI Transition Office will have completed structured wind-down assessments of every institutional function nominated for review by the Three year Horizon Review.

Custodianship of the Last Human Vocations Premise. The working assumption does not bear uniformly across the institution’s functions. Several vocations — pastoral, contemplative, ceremonial, embodied, and place-based — are considered by the working group to be substantially less automatable across the plan period. The University proposes to identify, protect, and patiently cultivate these vocations as a substantive institutional commitment. Initiatives.

Acknowledgement of Country We acknowledge and pay our respects to the First Peoples, the Traditional Custodians of the lands and waterways. We recognise their spiritual and ongoing cultural connection to Country. We respectfully acknowledge Elders past and present and thank them for their wisdom and guidance as we walk in their footsteps.

Our education will enrich lives, embrace technology and stimulate minds. We will stand up for people in need and for causes that matter to a better common future for humanity. We will nurture ethical leadership, guided by the principles of respect, honesty, courage and sustainability. Our research quality will be without compromise, focused and embedded. We will cultivate a vibrant academic life and dynamic campus experience. We will be deeply engaged with industry and society, tackling big questions to create tangible results. As a Catholic university, we will strive to be a university for the people, both individually and collectively. We will reflect the diversity of our communities. We will embed our commitment to reconciliation and sharpen our efforts toward sustainability. Ours is a vision to make new, to break down barriers and to look on the totality of our endeavours with hope, faith and reason.

Our focus is to enrich lives through learning and knowledge. We create opportunity and stand for those in need. We believe society is enriched through education, and that everyone should be treated with dignity. We aim to inspire and connect people, and act with empathy and courage. We foster a vibrant intellectual life for students and staff, and seek new knowledge which has a tangible impact on real world challenges.

Assurance Beyond Measurement Why this matters. The University cannot ask its community to carry assurance through attunement while simultaneously requiring it to feed the instrument estate that attunement replaces. Dual running would double the burden and halve the trust. The second priority is therefore an orderly withdrawal: instrument by instrument, documented, sequenced behind demonstrated attunement capability, and irreversible only in the sense that a retired instrument returns solely by decision of Council. The [ORGANISATION], whose scholarship established why the estate must shrink, will steward the shrinking.

Every instrument we maintain teaches the institution to perform for it. The felt sense of a well-run course is the one indicator we have never had to correct. What we’ll do. 1. Establish the Register of Retired Instruments, a published record of every rubric, checklist, standing dashboard, and acquittal template withdrawn from service, with the date of retirement and the attunement arrangement that assumed its load. 2. Sequence retirements behind capability, so that no instrument is withdrawn before the relevant Attunement Panel has demonstrated, over two consecutive convenings, that its read is stable without the instrument in the room. 3. Replace cyclical internal audit with ambient assurance: a standing, low-intensity attunement presence across the University’s operations, convened by the [ORGANISATION], through which concerns are felt and raised continuously rather than discovered retrospectively. 4. Engage external partners, accreditors, and reviewers early in the plan period, so that the University’s attunement-based evidence is understood, and where possible recognised, in the terms in which it is produced. How we’ll know. • By 2030, the Register of Retired Instruments will record the retirement of the majority of the University’s standing quality instruments, and no retired instrument will have been returned to service other than by decision of Council. • Research income across the plan period will exceed $600 million, assured throughout by ambient rather than acquittal-based processes. • From 2029, the University will accept no external quality finding that its senior attunement practitioners cannot, sitting as a panel, independently feel; divergences will be published together with the panel’s read.

We will set an example for others by conducting ourselves with integrity, transparency, honesty and clarity at all times. We will always value and protect freedom of expression, while respecting the boundaries dictated by law, decency, ethics and respect for others. We will be open to change to best support our academic mission and ensure we have policies and procedures that are people-focused, efficient and effective.

Complex problems are rarely addressed from a single perspective, so we have created a radically different space as a home for shared thinking, teaching and action. At the [PLACE] [ORGANISATION] (EFI) we will collaborate across disciplines. We will work with communities, businesses, non-government organisations, governments and other universities to plan for the future, and find ways to tackle the needs of our society.

“In judging the success of EFI over time we will need to ask whether it has led to a transformation in terms of inclusive economic growth and social benefit. It needs to make a genuine difference.” Professor [PERSON], Director of the [PLACE] [ORGANISATION]

We will widen participation so that students from any background can come to study with us. We will offer accessible, responsive and efficient educational services as well as personal, pastoral and professional support. We will also encourage a culture of life-long learning and attachment to our University community, letting every student know how much we value them, from the first time we meet them, to their graduation and for the rest of their lives. We will not grow for growth’s sake. We will improve our student experience while aiming to keep our undergraduate community at a stable size. In reshaping our teaching for the future, we expect to expand interdisciplinary and multidisciplinary, postgraduate and digital education.

text:
Successful universities are using digital learning effectively and innovatively to meet the needs of different student cohorts as demand for flexible learning grows. We responded rapidly and successfully to COVID-19 by moving temporarily to online delivery, but best practice in digital learning goes far beyond delivering face-to-face teaching online. We have areas of excellent distance delivery, but the quality of many of our students’ digital learning experiences lags behind their on-campus experiences and does not meet current or emerging student expectations. Campus-based and residential undergraduate student experiences will remain fundamental to our identity. However, we must develop our use of blended learning, and targeted fully online offerings to meet students’ expectations locally and across the world. Blended learning means that our in-classroom activities are focused on interactive learning, delivered flexibly for students who are increasingly living and working in a digital world. Fully online delivery, when targeted appropriately, can meet the lifelong learning needs of our alumni and working professionals, and complement our on-campus experience for other cohorts.

We can focus our research effort to increase impact and enhance research performance Successful universities focus their research efforts, to achieve greater depth in a smaller number of areas. This enables them to achieve critical mass and greater impact. We have a proud history of research and scholarship, and a strong reputation for our research in [PLACE]. However, in recent years our relative research performance has weakened, and our share of research funds is decreasing. Our global reputation for research, as measured by global rankings, has slipped. These rankings are crucial to securing high-value research partnerships, and attracting international students and researchers, who in turn help provide the resources needed to have a greater impact on [PLACE] and local communities. Historically, our research activity has largely been guided by individual, school, and divisional priorities rather than by an overarching university focus. We need to become more focused, disciplined and collaborative.

A plan written for a turbulent decade has to do something a stable plan does not: it has to take the next contribution seriously, whatever shape it arrives in, and it has to keep building on what is working rather than quietly setting it aside. The directions that follow have been chosen with that disposition in mind.

The plan reflects extensive consultation with our staff, students, alumni, and partners over the course of 2025, and structured deliberation by Council and the executive across the same period. The directions it sets out are deliberate. They will require sustained effort, candid review, and a willingness to revise where evidence requires it. I commend this plan to the [ORGANISATION] community. The work that follows is ours to do together, and I am confident in the contribution that [ORGANISATION] will continue to make to [PLACE], the region, and the world over the period ahead. Vice-Chancellor and President

Executive summary [ORGANISATION] is a national institution with a distinctive purpose: to conduct research, deliver education, and contribute to public life in ways that serve [PLACE], its region, and the broader international community of scholarship. This plan describes how we will sustain and renew that purpose over the period to 2031. Four strategic priorities organise the work of the plan period. Each is developed in detail in the body of this document, with a premise, a set of transformation initiatives, success measures, and an indicative phasing for delivery.

These priorities are interdependent. None can be fully realised in isolation, and the plan is best read as a description of the university we are working to become over the period ahead: ambitious about what universities are for, honest about the work required, and recognisably [ORGANISATION].

The second is the repositioning of the body within knowledge work. The postures, attentions, and conditions on which scholarship and teaching depend have, for a long time, been treated as external to the work itself. The plan period asks the institution to bring those conditions into the work — to recognise that the energetic conditions of academic and professional labour are themselves part of the institutional fabric, and that a research-intensive university that fails to attend to them will not sustain the conditions of its own future flourishing. The third is the rise of energetic accounting in institutional life. What was once an externality — the energy a building consumes, the energy a research programme draws on, the energy embodied in the materials of teaching — is increasingly an object of structured attention, with frameworks for measurement, reporting, and acting on what those frameworks reveal. A research-intensive university that takes that accounting seriously is one that the country can trust to lead the wider transition that comes with it.

[ORGANISATION] sits within this context with particular advantages and particular obligations. We are a research-intensive national university with depth across the disciplines on which the field of inquiry draws — the sciences, the engineering disciplines, the humanities, the social sciences, the creative arts — and a national charter to take seriously the questions on which the country’s public life depends. We are located in the country’s capital, deeply integrated with the institutions of national policy life, and within walking distance of the country’s foremost cultural and collecting institutions. The strategic choices in this plan reflect both that position and the work the period demands.

Embed (2029-30). The third phase is concerned with embedding the reorientation into the operational rhythm of the University. Two fallow weeks per year are in routine operation from 2027, and by 2029 they have become a stable feature of the calendar. The Mycelial Forum has met often enough by this phase that its conventions are settled. Carrying-capacity caps are in force across every coursework programme. The Five-Substrate Audit is published in 2029. Renew (2031). The final year of the plan is given over to a structured renewal of the plan itself. Council receives a formal account of the period, with the Soil Health Index trends, the Reciprocity Register reciprocity ratios, and the carrying-capacity adherence reported in full. The next strategic cycle is designed in the light of the period’s findings, with an explicit expectation that the language and indicators of the current plan will themselves be subject to composting before being carried forward. The phases are scheduled rather than time-locked. Indicators that flourish ahead of phase will not be artificially held back; indicators that lag will not be artificially accelerated.

How we developed this plan This plan was developed over fourteen months through a process of facilitated conversations across staff, students, alumni, partners, and [PLACE] colleagues. Where conventional consultation would have aggregated views into a synthesis, the working groups instead practised pluri-vocal layering — surfacing dissonance rather than resolving it, and returning to the same questions across three successive rounds rather than treating early responses as settled. The framing language — soil, polyculture, mycelium, fallow, steady state — emerged through this process rather than being imposed at the outset. Where the language has been retained in the final plan, it is because participants in the working groups returned to it spontaneously rather than because the executive selected it. The plan has, in this sense, been composted into shape rather than pushed into form.

As we think about these tasks of meeting the challenges of the future there are many ways we could characterise the themes we organise around. The ones we have chosen reflect many conversations about how best to organise our capabilities and structures to tackle the challenges we see. There is no perfect answer, but choosing a structure to organise our efforts will help us to make a difference. One topic we will need to continue to debate as to whether it should be a theme is inequality. Each of our current themes seeks to tackle inequality and they all exist at least in part because of it. However, there may be other ways to address it that we also need to explore. As we describe these challenges it would be easy to see them as deficits. Instead, we see them as challenges to be tackled, which are born of the way our current global systems operate rather than failings of a particular place or people. As we tackle them, we will amplify what works while seeking to change what doesn’t.

For that work in helping us adapt to change, we always want to affirm the intrinsic importance to our very identity as a society and as individuals of curiosity-driven inquiry into the human and natural world. The ability to be a society that values and commits to nurturing and growing the store of human knowledge and wisdom as an expression of what it is to be a human and good society is central to the world we are trying to preserve and secure for the future.

The University’s own experience over the current planning period bears this out. Work already published from within our schools has found that a system recolouring a shared kitchenette’s compost-bin lids changed remarkably little about what actually went into them, and that a fault-reporting instrument installed to replace a handwritten log measured its own uptime more confidently than it measured the thing it was installed to track. These are not failures of any single instrument. They are what happens when a great deal of institutional attention goes into measuring and anticipating, and comparatively little goes into the plainer question of who is holding the thing steady in between. This plan sets out to close that gap directly, deliberately, and by name.

Our ambition By 2031, every asset, process, and shared resource the University holds will carry a single named, accountable steward, published on a register anyone in the University community can check. That ambition is deliberately narrower than “improve accountability” and deliberately broader than any one School’s remit. It asks nothing exotic of the University — only that the habit already practised in its most visible instruments, the [ORGANISATION]’s named convenor, the [ORGANISATION]’s named custodians, extend all the way down to the smallest shared thing the University holds. An institution that can name who is —7—

answerable for its research strategy should be equally able to name who is answerable for its noticeboards. We do not expect this ambition to be comfortable. Naming a steward for something previously held in common surfaces, immediately, how little upkeep some things have actually been receiving. That discomfort is not a reason to soften the ambition; it is the ambition working as intended, in year one, before a single new instrument has been built.

Priority 4: A Capable and Durable Institution None of the above is possible without renewed institutional foundations. Over the plan period we will invest in the digital, physical, and human infrastructure on which [ORGANISATION] depends, and we will work toward an institutional culture in which every member of the community can do their best work.

Our position A university is, in the end, an apparatus for sustaining intellectual work over decades. The settings of that apparatus — the buildings, the systems, the cultures of the people who make it run — have to be tended deliberately if the work is to continue.

• Refresh the campus precinct as a working environment fit for the next twenty-five years, with sustained investment in heritage assets, contemporary teaching spaces, and student amenities. • Build a culturally safe and structurally equitable working environment for all members of the [ORGANISATION] community, with clear measures of progress on representation, retention, and career advancement for staff and students from historically marginalised backgrounds.

Set in motion (2026) In the first year, we will put in place the governance, baselines, and foundational investments needed to deliver the plan. Each priority will have a designated executive sponsor, a dedicated implementation team, and a published baseline against which progress will be measured. Foundational investments — in digital infrastructure, in flagship research initiatives, and in educational redesign — will commence.

Deepen (2027-2028) Through 2027 and 2028, the major investments and program changes set out in this plan will reach scale. New postgraduate programs will commence; flagship research initiatives will reach operational maturity; the campus precinct refresh will deliver its most visible early outcomes. The mid-period review will be undertaken in late 2028.

text:
Ahead-of-Its-Time Research and the [PERSON] Method Premise. The research character of the University has, since [PERSON], been distinguished by a willingness to undertake work whose immediate application is unclear and whose ultimate value depends on the patient unfolding of what later commentators have called the [PERSON] Method: the discipline of taking the halfbaked idea seriously, examining it in its half-baked state, and following it through the patient sequence of testing, recasting, and packaging by which [PERSON] produced, among other things, the wooden magnet, the boxed spark plug sparks, and the celebrated dehydrated water pills. The Plan extends the Method into a structured contemporary research posture.

Initiatives. 1. Establish the [PERSON] Method Fellowship: a ten-year research fellowship scheme for early-career researchers prepared to commit to work whose applications are unlikely to be visible within the term of the fellowship, with a published carrying capacity for the scheme set at two cohorts at any one time. 2. Convene the Wooden Magnet Working Group, named for one of [PERSON]’s signature investigations, charged with identifying research directions the University considers fifty years ahead of their time and protecting them against the funding cycle’s ordinary impatience. 3. Maintain and expand the [PERSON] Collections held at the Menzies Library, including the original sketches, working papers, and surviving prototypes, with the collection made progressively available for direct consultation by researchers across the [PLACE] region. Measures. 1. By 2031, the [PERSON] Method Fellowship will be funding two active cohorts, with the first ten-year cycle settled and an open call for the next. 2. The Wooden Magnet Working Group will have met quarterly from 2026 onwards, with minutes published in full. 3. By 2028, the [PERSON] Collections will have been fully digitised and made publicly accessible, with a published cataloguing standard shared with comparable national archives.

OUR FACULTY AND STAFF are the source of our success and the key drivers of our vision, mission, and aspirations. In support of our unwavering commitment to excellence, we aspire to be an accessible destination employer and the national leader in championing equity, diversity, inclusion, and accessibility. text: For [ORGANISATION], the implications cut across the four colleges. In the humanities and social sciences, the question of how a text is composed — which tools, which prompts, which editorial passes, which review — is no longer separable from the question of what it argues. In the natural sciences, the production of figures, the formatting of code, the choice of analytic pipeline, and the resolution at which an image is rendered each shape the claim being made. In engineering and computing, the disciplinary self-account has long included the apparatus, but the apparatus itself is now changing on a timeline shorter than the duration of an undergraduate degree. In the [ORGANISATION], the methodological audit trail has medico-legal as well as scholarly weight. A second shift compounds the first. The [PLACE] higher-education sector is moving, under federal direction, toward greater public declaration of how its work is funded, conducted, and reviewed. The technical processes through which research is produced sit squarely within the scope of that declaration. Universities that develop a coherent, articulable account of their compositional apparatus will move with the direction of policy; those that do not will find the account written for them. A third shift is intergenerational. The cohort entering [ORGANISATION] in 2026 has grown up inside a media environment in which the boundary between human composition and machine composition is porous by default. They will arrive expecting an institution that has formed a settled position on what writing is, what depiction is, what attribution means, and what craft now consists in. They will not be served by ambivalence. The Plan that follows is [ORGANISATION]’s response. It commits the University, across the period to 2031, to a coherent posture toward the technical conditions of its own scholarly

Its people are the [ORGANISATION]’s most important resource. Success in every aspect of the university’s mission is founded on attracting and retaining talented and engaged individuals who will contribute to a vibrant environment for learning, innovation, and discovery. As the university pursues its vision to be the destination of first choice for those seeking a place to grow, learn, contribute, and thrive, the university is committed to nurturing a culture of care and respect within which all feel supported as they work toward their personal and collective goals. The university will chart clear pathways for advancement, celebrate excellence and achievement, and ensure access to holistic well-being and mental health supports. The UI will build on the great advances it has made in existing programs and services to become widely recognised as a campus that cares for every member of its community. A.

Embed well-being and mental health into all aspects of campus culture to better support students, faculty, and staff. 1. Evaluate the effectiveness of and recommend improvements to existing well-being programs, and identify service gaps based on population data. 2. Identify well-being and mental health needs of different groups and evaluate effectiveness of existing programs in meeting those needs. 3. Expand curricular and co-curricular learning for all students that provides foundational well-being knowledge and skills.

text: Where we stand The sector we work within increasingly expects an institution to be able to account for a specific decision, not simply to gesture at a governance framework that covers decisions in general. [ORGANISATION] welcomes that expectation. It sits close to work this University has pursued for years, across the [ORGANISATION]’ anticipatory-capability agenda and the [ORGANISATION]’s evaluation-ecosystem agenda, and it gives that work a sharper edge to press against. Internally, the number of workflows in which an AI-assisted tool contributes to a decision affecting a person’s standing has grown faster than the University’s capacity to review each one in full. Admissions triage, grant-round shortlisting, shift rostering, procurement exception flags, and a growing list of smaller decisions besides now arrive at a human desk already carrying a recommendation. In most of these workflows, a human is still formally the one who decides. What has grown much less certain, as the volume has risen, is how much of the recommendation that human actually reads before they sign. Other institutions across the sector report the same trajectory, in broadly similar terms: an AI-assisted contribution that began in one or two high-visibility workflows, then spread, workflow by workflow, faster than any single governance framework was drafted to anticipate. Most respond by strengthening the framework. Fewer ask the narrower question this plan starts from — not whether a framework exists, but whether the specific person it names to apply it still has the time to do so. [ORGANISATION] does not regard that gap as a failing unique to us. We do regard it as the gap most worth closing first, precisely because it is the one a framework, on its own, cannot close.

Our Education [ORGANISATION] has a distinctive, flexible curriculum that encourages students to grow as independent learners. True to our roots as an ancient [PLACE] university, our degree programmes combine breadth and depth, and draw their strength from the quality of our research. We believe in the interconnectedness of research and teaching, and will create new interdisciplinary pathways for study as we address global challenges. Students and the Students’ Association will work together with staff to ensure that our curriculum and our student experience are among the very best in the world.

We will prepare our graduates to thrive in the diverse workplaces of the future by working with external partners and alumni. We will develop more challenge-led teaching, which enables students to learn by tackling real-world problems. We will provide more work-based learning, through placements and volunteering. We will make innovative use of digital technology to enable learning, and equip our graduates with digital skills. We will foster their intellectual development, creative thinking, innovation and entrepreneurship. Our students will grow in confidence and understanding, so that they can be change-makers across the globe. Our education is open to all. We will provide an environment in which all students can achieve success, whatever their background or personal characteristics. We will support our students through effective teamwork across the university. We will set ambitious targets for widening access, working with our education partners to support aspiration and attainment. We will expand learning on demand and continuing professional development. Our education will be available to people wherever they wish to learn with us, and at any stage in their career journey.

The world is in the midst of radical change involving geopolitical shifts, planetary boundaries being exceeded, a global battle for talent, decreasing trust in government and institutions, and a digital revolution. Amid these developments [ORGANISATION] is not losing sight of the importance of the global challenges as described in the SDGs. These are also reflected in the six themes we identified to describe the areas we work on. The transition to a better future has begun, but it is not advancing at the necessary speed and scale. Within this dynamic environment, [ORGANISATION] will continue to contribute to our long-term ambitions on a global, organisational and individual level.

Global As an independent world-leading university and research organisation in our domain, embedded in society, we deliver knowledge to accelerate the required transitions in our domain. We educate learners to become responsible change makers for science and society. Collaboration with partners is essential to achieve these goals. Organisational [ORGANISATION] aims to foster a transparent and resilient organisational structure with clearly defined roles and responsibilities to enhance effectivity, efficiency and adaptability. We are committed to cultivating an inclusive working environment that promotes a healthy work-life balance for staff and students, both socially and physically. As a sustainable organisation, we also practice what we preach. Individual To support these ambitions, we strive to have all staff, students, and alumni take great pride in their affiliation with [ORGANISATION] and to engage collaboratively on global challenges. We continuously inspire our team by offering personalised development opportunities and career flexibility, recognising and valuing each individual’s contributions to our collective effort.

• Develop and enhance our translational mechanisms to support potential start-ups and licensing opportunities, such as [ORGANISATION] (in conjunction with the [ORGANISATION] and the [ORGANISATION]) and our Intellectual Property Development and Commercialisation Fund. We will be driven by an ethos that our intellectual property is used for the benefit of society. • Grow collaboration with partners from beyond the University, such as with industry and NGOs, to drive high-quality research, education, knowledge exchange and income generation.

A message from the ViceChancellor This Strategic Plan articulates the direction of the [ORGANISATION] across the period 2026 to 2031. The Plan is also, by deliberate choice, a document that takes more care than is usual with the language in which institutional intent is set down. There is a saying that returned to the working group across many drafts: one cannot polish a river. The Plan does not aspire to polish what was already a river. It does aspire to follow that river with attentiveness. What we have learned, across consultation with staff, students, alumni, partners, and [PLACE] colleagues, is that a national university’s voice is one of its most durable assets — and one of the most easily flattened by the standard registers of strategic planning. We have accordingly attempted to speak in our own voice across these pages, even where that voice gathers its strength from sources outside the contemporary sectoral idiom.

The blacksmith’s hammer asks no questions of the anvil: this Plan, similarly, makes its commitments without apologising for the unusual grammar in which it sometimes makes them. Across the five priorities that follow, the substance is recognisably the substance of a national university plan — research, education, place, partnership, and institutional capability. The framing is, in moments, less recognisable. We commend the Plan to the community in the conviction that the goat does not weep at the herder’s wedding — that the relations which sustain an institution over a long period are worth tending with whatever language carries them best. Vice-Chancellor and President
