Learning from history The past, and specifically our own eventful history, which is closely linked to [PLACE]’s fate, offers numerous opportunities to understand the development of our identity in a broader context and to gain valuable insights for the future. For this reason, it is particularly important for us to know our history and continuously reflect on it - critically, factually, without embellishment, but also with pride in our achievements and accomplishments.

Political neutrality and academic freedom [ORGANISATION] is a place of free thought and open scientific discourse. In the tradition of great universities, it is committed to providing a platform for critical reflection, debate, and intellectual diversity. As an institution, [ORGANISATION] remains politically neutral and does not take partisan positions. However, political neutrality does not mean indifference: where science is attacked or instrumentalized, we defend fact-based knowledge against ideology and "alternative truths". At the same time, [ORGANISATION] protects and promotes freedom of expression and the open exchange of scientific knowledge. We firmly believe that free science is not only the foundation for technical progress but also essential for a resilient and democratic society.

Challenges & opportunities Current challenges at [ORGANISATION] During the fuTUre fit process, we placed particular emphasis on capturing the current situation in a nuanced way and from multiple perspectives. The reports from the working groups and the fuTUre fit Convention have confirmed known challenges and revealed new areas for action. Our goal is to act in a maximally solution-oriented and forward-thinking manner. This is precisely why a strategy must clearly name realities and reflect the courage to tackle challenges decisively. This chapter reflects that approach. The following overview highlights key challenges that are already relevant today and will become even more important in the coming years. Lack of international visibility 

university worth the country’s investment. The Plan accordingly proposes a measured rebalancing. The fifth context is the most particular: the conditions of place. The University sits on [PLACE] and [PLACE]-[PLACE] Country, in the federal capital, in a city whose lake, hills, and weather are part of the institutional formation of every cohort that passes through. The lake does not apologise for its depth. The Plan attends to place not as a backdrop but as a constitutive element of the University’s distinctiveness, and one which will, across the period covered by this Plan, be more deliberately tended than it has been over the previous several planning cycles. Read together, these five contexts ask the University to articulate its purpose in a register that is more deliberately particular than the sectoral norm. The framing this Plan adopts — including the occasional reach for sayings that have come up across consultation and that participants returned to spontaneously — reflects a working conviction: a borrowed shadow does not cool the borrower. The University will speak in its own voice across the period of this Plan.

Where we are headed By 2031, [ORGANISATION] will be a national university recognised — within the country and in its region — for the depth of its scholarship, the quality of its teaching, and the unmistakable character of its institutional voice. We do not lend the well its own water: the University’s contribution to public life in 2031 will draw on the deep, particular resources of the institution rather than on the borrowed forms of the moment. The Plan describes how that voice will be cultivated across research, teaching, partnership, place, and institutional capability over the period 2026 to 2031. Even the salt remembers the sea: the University, in 2031, will recognisably be the institution it has long been, in better condition than it received itself, and oriented toward the long century ahead.

[PLACE] University is embedded in the communities we serve across regional [PLACE]. This place-based approach is central to who we are and shapes our priorities, partnerships and the way we deliver education and research. At the same time, it is important that we have a global reach to create opportunities for our students, staff and regions.

Driver 6 Fostering an inclusive and rewarding workplace: Delivering rewarding careers that make a difference in a workplace that values people. Our staff drive our success. When we support our people to excel, they deliver world-class teaching, research and support, benefiting learners and communities directly. We will embed lifelong learning at every level. Staff have access to ongoing development, training in emerging technologies and clear career pathways. Through our Co-op model, we’ll offer our students opportunities to build a future with us. We’ll enable staff exchanges between partners, our institutes and TAFE, embedding co-design and co-teaching, sharing knowledge and building innovative curriculum. These placements bring real-world experience and fresh insights back to campus, keeping our programs relevant and our people at the forefront of digital literacy and industry practice.

To attract and retain top talent, we offer an inclusive, rewarding workplace that values diversity, collaboration and flexibility. We’re modernising systems, investing in campuses and technology, and supporting wellbeing, so our people have the tools and environment to thrive. Recognition and reward programs celebrate excellence and innovation, reinforcing that careers flourish here. We foster a culture of safety, accountability and awareness to ensure our campuses and services are safe, inclusive and welcoming for all, particularly children and young people. [PLACE] will be known as a university where great people come and stay – because they can grow, innovate and make a real difference.

Expand the importance and impact of our research on [PLACE], the nation, and the planet The large scale and rich diversity of [PLACE] provide an exceptional opportunity to create and to observe in depth the impacts of our research. The well-developed extension activities that are integral to our land-, sea-, and space-grant missions have enabled translation of our research into practice. We can expand, enhance, and adapt these activities throughout the state so that mutually beneficial engagement of our expertise and research can change and improve lives in communities around the world. While continuing our long standing interactions with rural communities, our research, engagement, and partnerships with underserved urban populations can enhance the impact and diversity of our scholarship and enrich the experience of our students. Communities of all sizes can benefit by helping us to translate our work on global challenges to the local scale.

Faculty Key Performance Indicators 1. Increase the retention of faculty on the tenure track, close equity gaps, and remove barriers to success. 2. Increase by 20% the number of faculty with prestigious and highly prestigious awards. 3. Increase by 20% the national and international recognition of our faculty as educators. 4. Increase proportion of tenure track faculty to 65%.

• Extending knowledge in all its forms (e.g., leadership training, continuing education, workforce development) to benefit communities and constituencies beyond the university; • Meeting issues where they exist. We will utilise the knowledge we gain through discovery and innovation to meet the needs of [PLACE] citizens in rural and urban communities; • Sharing and applying our research discoveries and innovations through knowledge transfer, commercialisation, and partnerships.

Translation, Provenance, and the Crossing Premise. The work of moving between analogue and digital substrates — the digitisation of a physical archive, the printing of a generative work, the encoding of a field instrument, the materialisation of a simulation — is itself scholarship that the University has rarely articulated as such. [ORGANISATION] will treat translation across the crossing as a primary scholarly object. Initiatives. 1. The [ORGANISATION] Translation Office will be established, reporting to the Deputy ViceChancellor (Research), to maintain the institution’s register of analogue-digital translations and to convene methodological renewal across the disciplines that practise them. 2. The University will publish, annually, the [ORGANISATION] Provenance Standard for analogue digital translation, intended for institutional use and made openly available to the broader [PLACE] higher-education sector. Measures. • One hundred per cent of [ORGANISATION] institutional digitisation projects initiated from 2027 will comply with the [ORGANISATION] Provenance Standard, with no exception sustained for more than a single audit cycle. • The Translation Office will release a Translation Inventory annually from 2028, including custodianship, intended-use envelope, and provenance metadata per entry. • A published five-year audit of analogue-digital translation practice across the four colleges, released in 2031 to inform the strategic cycle that follows.

Phasing Delivery proceeds across four phases spanning the period 2026 to 2031 contiguously. Each phase carries a defined posture and a defined relationship to the five strategic priorities. Foundation 2026. The Hybrid Substrate Institute, the three Crossing Studios, the Computational Literacy Programme, the Computational Companion fellowship scheme, and the Translation Office are stood up across the first year of the Plan. Inaugural directors are appointed; foundational frameworks (the Material Reasoning Capability Framework, the Computational Literacy Framework, the [ORGANISATION] Provenance Standard) are released in draft for community consultation; the inaugural Hybrid Substrate Convention is scheduled for 2027 and partner institutions are confirmed.

Writing as Engineered Practice Context. Writing at the University — student, scholarly, professional, administrative — is increasingly co-produced with technical systems whose contribution is rarely articulated. [ORGANISATION] will treat the writing apparatus of the institution as scholarship, not infrastructure, and will articulate it for use by the University community and for the broader sector.

Commitments. 1. The University will stand up the Centre for Composition Studies, anchored in the School of Literature, Languages and Linguistics with cross-appointments held jointly across the School of Computing and the [ORGANISATION] & [PLACE]. 2. A “Writing Apparatus” elective stream will be developed and made available to every undergraduate degree program, with a minimum of three sequenced units offered each semester from 2028. 3. The University will establish the [ORGANISATION] Editorial Stack: an institution-wide articulation of accepted, declared, and prohibited writing tools by use class, published openly and revised at twelve-month intervals. Indicators. • One hundred per cent of taught course work at 2000 level and above will publish a “writing apparatus” disclosure to students alongside the standard course outline by 2029. • Three peer-reviewed monographs per year will be published through [ORGANISATION] Press in the Composition Studies series by 2029, sustained through the remainder of the plan period. • An annual [ORGANISATION] Composition Prize, awarded in three categories (drafting, revision, machine-assisted composition), each with a published methodological declaration as a condition of submission.

Visual Composition in Hybrid Media Context. The visual artefacts produced by the institution — figures, diagrams, posters, slides, video, generative output, exhibition materials — pass through compounding technical stacks whose contribution to the eventual artefact is generally invisible to the reader or viewer. [ORGANISATION] will own the visual stack as a site of scholarship and craft.

To deliver on our purpose to benefit society, we must ensure we have the right capabilities and resources available to succeed. This means we must equip our people with the required skills, knowledge and resources, working together with the systems and supports that ensure we deliver lasting impact and benefit for the communities we serve.

We will create environments for staff to strive for and deliver excellence. By continuing to pursue and demonstrate the highest standards of scholarship and performance, we will maintain the confidence of our students, staff and communities.

Reaffirming students at the heart of our academic mission, we will create an environment where every student, regardless of background, can flourish. Through our distinctive curriculum, underpinned by an outstanding oncampus experience, our students will take charge of their own learning, and develop the analytical skills and mindset needed for a rapidly changing world.

To achieve our ambitions we must ensure our financial and operational sustainability. Through organisational rigour, integrity and a stronger prioritisation of effort and investment, we will ensure the long-term resilience and success of our university.

By 2030 we will have strengthened our long-term financial sustainability and improved our ability to respond to our changing world. We will have improved the effectiveness and efficiency of how we work together, and improved staff engagement and satisfaction.

Looking beyond 2030, we will continue to lead with purpose and create meaningful value. We will be responsive to the changing needs of our students and society. We will be bold in our pursuit of knowledge, resilience, and the transformative impact of education and research.

Our targets 1. Undergraduate satisfaction sustained in the top quartile of [PLACE] universities across the plan period. 2. Priority 3: Belonging, Place, and Reconciliation Universities flourish through their relationships with the communities they serve — and they fail when those relationships are characterised by extraction rather than partnership. Across the plan period we will deepen our engagement, take honest steps toward reconciliation, and build the conditions for belonging across the [ORGANISATION] community.

Our position [ORGANISATION] was founded to serve the nation, and the meaning of that service has continued to deepen across the university’s history. The decade ahead requires us to honour that founding intent through sustained, patient, honest partnership — with [PLACE] communities, with the [PLACE] public service, and with the publics that have always been the university’s reason for being.

Our actions 1. Move beyond first-generation reconciliation work toward structural transformation, including a renewed [ORGANISATION], sustained investment in [PLACE]-led research, and a long-term commitment to truth telling about the university’s own history. 2. Deepen engagement with the [PLACE] public service, including through expansion of executive education, renewal of long-running partnerships with policy agencies, and a sustained programme of evidence-based contribution to national decision-making. 3. Our Research Throughout the centuries, researchers at the [ORGANISATION] have generated new insights in medicine, science and engineering, law, social sciences, arts and humanities. Our work has earned many honours and awards, and has contributed to five Nobel prizes. Like our education, our research will be intellectually rigorous. Whether working within our established areas of excellence, or developing interdisciplinary approaches that generate new methods of inquiry, we will tackle theoretical and practical problems. We will generate new knowledge and will connect and combine ideas, addressing economic and societal issues with ambition and imagination.

Our research will be globally excellent and locally relevant. To ensure this, we will engage with our external partners as we plan for the future, and will work collaboratively with them both on and off campus. Our research will be open to all. We will work to share our findings, and to promote open access to academic resources for anyone who wishes to learn. Our research will have impact on our world, and will inform our curriculum, shaping what and how we teach. We will train and support the next generation of researchers, equipping them with the skills they need to develop their expertise and to engage with the challenges of the future.

In these pages, we set out 20 commitments across these four themes. We will address five great challenges of our age. As the digital revolution brings new opportunities, and the climate emergency threatens us all, we commit to delivering outstanding education and research that will shape the lives of our students, and tackle the pressing problems of our world.

[ORGANISATION]’s place in the national interest has never depended on the size of its ambitions but on the University’s willingness to be specific about them, and to be answerable when a trajectory it backed does not arrive. This plan is that answerability, written down in advance. — Vice-Chancellor and President

Executive summary This plan commits [ORGANISATION] to a single working principle across the decade ahead: no commitment — to a person, a cohort, or a partner — is made, or continued, without evidence of the trajectory that justifies it. Four strategic pillars carry that principle from the moment an offer is drafted through to the moment a portfolio of evidence is finally retired.

Together, these pillars close a gap the University has lived with for longer than it has been comfortable admitting: that a trajectory, once backed, was rarely checked again. By 2031, evidence of trajectory will accompany every commitment [ORGANISATION] makes and every commitment it renews, reviewed on a cadence the institution publishes and holds itself to.

is backed, and a discipline for checking, on schedule, that the trajectory is still the one the University thought it was. Other institutions have reached for the same instinct without the same discipline, and the difference shows. A screening step added in response to a single bad outcome, then never revisited, is not evidence practice; it is sediment. [ORGANISATION]’s contribution to this moment is to treat the evidence itself as something to be designed, resourced, and eventually retired — not simply accumulated each time a panel or committee decides it wants to know more before it commits.

Renewing society by art, creativity and design Art, design and creativity drive innovation and entrepreneurship. These concepts radically question and challenge our society and culture. They generate new knowledge and understanding and create value by leveraging humane designs and viable solutions. To reap such rewards, we will develop and promote art-based activities across the boundaries of diverse disciplines, knowledge frameworks and communities.

Educating game changers Grand challenges call for the education of professionals with the knowledge and capabilities to build a sustainable society and to increase wellbeing through disruptive change. These capabilities need to be rooted in disciplinary excellence augmented by art, creativity, multidisciplinary collaboration and entrepreneurship. The development of programs toward integrative thinking and practices to engage students in societal challenges will improve the relevance of our education. We will increase the international exchange opportunities for our students.

Transforming our campus into a unique collaboration hub Our open and experimental collaboration ecosystem will attract students, faculty, staff and partners worldwide. The campus, with its state-of-the-art research and learning environment, is recognised for optimally supporting the production of new knowledge and innovation. We will build a vibrant campus centre that offers attractive opportunities for partnering, collaboration and sharing ideas and experiences.

Excellence in advancing and supporting our core goals Enabling the core academic mission of the [ORGANISATION] community is our first priority. To compete globally for the best faculty, students, staff, partners and other stakeholders, we need to develop world-class conditions and an environment for research, art, education and collaboration. We will invest in sustainable, long-term resourcing of our strategic priorities, build practices to recognise achievement and develop streamlined support service solutions facilitating academic excellence.

The third is climate and sustainability. The decade ahead will see deepening pressure on natural systems and intensifying transitions across the energy, industrial, and social systems on which our communities depend. Universities are central to navigating these transitions — both through research and through the leadership they educate.

A distinctive position [ORGANISATION] sits in a particular place. We are [PLACE]’s national university, established by an Act of [PLACE] [ORGANISATION] with a charter to serve the nation. We are located in the country’s capital, deeply integrated with the institutions of national life. We are research-intensive at a scale and depth unmatched in the country. And we are home to research and teaching strengths — across the sciences, humanities, social sciences, and policy domains — that are genuinely globally distinctive. This position confers both opportunity and obligation. The opportunity is to make a contribution to the national effort that no other institution can. The obligation is to do so with the seriousness, the independence, and the strategic clarity that the country deserves from its national university. This plan describes how we will meet that obligation over the years to 2031.

A vision for [ORGANISATION] in 2031 By 2031, the [ORGANISATION] will be the world-leading university for the study of [PLACE] and its place in the [PLACE] — recognised globally for the depth of its research, the quality of its educational programs, and the durability of its contribution to national and regional life. This vision is ambitious and focused. It reflects our distinctive mission, our particular institutional strengths, and the moment in which we find ourselves. It is grounded in eight decades of demonstrated capacity and oriented toward the next.
